articles.title: Nunes Marques muda entendimento do TSE e inclui Novo em debates eleitorais | G1
articles.standfirst: Partido questionou portaria que estabeleceu candidatos com direito a participação nos debates a partir da representação no Congresso Nacional.
articles.summary: Partido questionou portaria que estabeleceu candidatos com direito a participação nos debates a partir da representação no Congresso Nacional.
articles.body:
O ministro Nunes Marques, presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), concedeu nesta terça-feira (29) liminar requerida pelo Partido Novo, alterando entendimento anterior do TSE que regulamenta os critérios de participação de partidos em debates eleitorais em emissoras de rádio e TV.

A decisão liminar (provisória) garante a participação dos candidatos do Partido Novo nos debates das Eleições de 2026 em todas as emissoras de rádio e TV a partir desta terça.

O ministro determinou que os candidatos do partido ao governo do Distrito Federal (DF), Kiko Caputo, e do Rio de Janeiro (RJ), André Marinho participem dos debates que serão realizados pela TV Globo nesta terça.

A decisão também beneficia o candidato a presidente pelo Novo, Romeu Zema.

Nunes Marques atendeu a um pedido feito pela legenda e alterou um entendimento do próprio TSE definido em julho, quando a legenda ficou de fora da chamada tabela de representatividade dos partidos políticos.

🔎 Essa tabela define a divisão do tempo de propaganda gratuita em rádio e televisão e a participação das candidaturas em debates durante a campanha. A portaria com a tabela considerou o número de parlamentares eleitos para a Câmara dos Deputados e para o Senado por partidos e federações que cumpriram os requisitos da cláusula de desempenho.

O partido alegou ao TSE que a resolução ampliou as restrições previstas na lei de normas das eleições. E que a Justiça eleitoral deveria considerar eventuais alterações decorrentes de novas totalizações realizadas até 20 de julho do ano eleitoral.

O Novo elegeu 3 deputados em 2022, mas dois se filiaram até 20 de julho deste ano.

Nunes Marques concordou com o partido. Segundo o presidente do TSE, a interpretação restritiva, que considera exclusivamente a legenda pela qual o parlamentar foi eleito, "termina por projetar sobre os debates uma limitação que a Constituição estabeleceu expressamente para outras finalidades”, como acesso a fundos eleitorais e debates.

"Embora a legislação possa estabelecer critérios objetivos de representatividade para assegurar a participação, sua interpretação não deve restringir o espaço de confronto público entre candidaturas além do que decorre da própria lei", disse Nunes Marques na decisão.

articles.title: PT diz que rivais deturpam fala de Lula sobre 'toque' em mulheres | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula tratava de saúde preventiva masculina, como exame de toque, e disse que mulheres "aprendem a tomar toque desde pequenas".
articles.summary: Lula tratava de saúde preventiva masculina, como exame de toque, e disse que mulheres "aprendem a tomar toque desde pequenas".
articles.body:
O PT divulgou uma nota à imprensa nesta terça-feira (29) após a repercussão de uma declaração do presidente Lula sobre a resistência dos homens ao exame de prevenção do câncer de próstata. Durante um comício em Belém, no Pará, Lula afirmou que “as mulheres aprendem a tomar toque desde quando são pequenas”.

“Porque o homem é covarde. O homem não gosta de fazer teste de próstata. Ele não gosta de toque. As mulheres aprendem a tomar toque desde quando são pequenas. O homem, não. Ele é cheio de trejeito. Ele não sabe que, quando tiver câncer de próstata, vão dar muito toque nele”, afirmou o presidente e candidato à reeleição na noite de segunda-feira (28).

Na nota, o PT afirmou que Lula “obviamente se referiu aos exames ginecológicos preventivos que fazem parte da cultura da saúde da mulher”.

O partido disse ainda que os homens resistem aos exames urológicos preventivos por causa de uma “cultura machista” e acusou apoiadores de Flávio Bolsonaro de retirarem a fala de contexto para alimentar o que chamou de “máquina de fake news”.

O partido afirmou ainda que adversários se aproveitaram para deturpar a fala como forma de "tentar tirar o foco da série de denúncias sobre Flávio Bolsonaro".

"A última denúncia contra Flávio revela suspeitas de recebimento de presentes frutos de corrupção, como o tal do relógio de luxo (Rolex). Mais uma ação do Gabinete do Ódio Bolsonarista que tira de contexto uma fala para alimentar a máquina de desinformação e Fake News", afirmou o partido.

A coligação da chapa presidencial de Lula, formada pelo PT, PCdoB e PV, entrou com uma ação no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) por publicações com "grave descontextualização da fala de Lula e a tentativa de atribuir cunho sexual e repudiante em contexto factual inexistente".

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro e Tarcísio fazem último ato de campanha em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio fará carreata entre Santa Bárbara d’Oeste e Americana, com participação de Tarcísio e aliados; escolha do interior é um aceno ao eleitorado da região.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro e Tarcísio de Freitas realizam carreata entre Santa Bárbara d’Oeste e Americana no último ato de campanha antes do primeiro turno.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro participa de evento de campanha na Baixada Fluminense — Foto: Reprodução TV Globo

O último ato de campanha antes do primeiro turno das eleições do candidato à presidência pelo PL, Flávio Bolsonaro , será realizado no interior de São Paulo.

Está prevista para sábado (3) uma carreata em Santa Bárbara d'Oeste na parte da manhã. Seguirá até a cidade de Americana, encerrando o ato no parque de eventos onde costuma ser realizada a festa do peão da cidade.

O governador Tarcísio de Freitas , que tenta a reeleição para o governo de São Paulo, e outros aliados vão acompanhá-lo nas agendas.

Havia uma previsão de que o ato final da campanha fosse realizado na capital, mas aliados avaliaram que a logística seria inviável. A escolha do local também é um aceno ao eleitorado da região.

Os candidatos podem realizar atos um dia antes do primeiro turno, mas com restrições. Entre as regras, que o ato seja realizado antes das 22h.

São Paulo foi um dos estados que Flávio focou na reta final de campanha. Na última sexta, foi ao rodeio em Jaguariúna, também no interior do estado. Na segunda (28) e na terça (29), ficou na capital.

articles.title: Pesquisas eleitorais: TSE exige mais detalhes e institutos criticam | G1
articles.standfirst: Ofício foi assinado pelo presidente da corte, ministro Nunes Marques. Mudanças valem a partir de 5 de outubro, um dia após o 1º turno, e exigem mais detalhes sobre metodologia, momento da coleta e eventuais substituições de entrevistados.
articles.summary: O TSE exigirá mais detalhes no registro de pesquisas eleitorais a partir de outubro, medida que gerou críticas de institutos sobre o momento e a falta de debate da mudança.
articles.body:
Prédio do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), em Brasília — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) mudou as regras para o registro de pesquisas eleitorais no Sistema de Registro de Pesquisas Eleitorais (PesqEle), sistema público de consulta a levantamentos de intenção de voto, e passou a exigir mais detalhes sobre a coleta de dados, a metodologia e os questionários. Institutos de pesquisa criticaram a adoção das novas exigências em meio ao processo eleitoral deste ano.

A alteração foi formalizada em ofício assinado pelo presidente do TSE, ministro Nunes Marques, em 17 de setembro. O documento estabelece que as novas regras valem para pesquisas registradas a partir de 5 de outubro, um dia após o primeiro turno. O ofício foi enviado aos representantes legais das empresas que realizam pesquisas eleitorais.

“As empresas continuarão realizando o preenchimento dos campos atualmente existentes no sistema e passarão a fornecer informações complementares destinadas a detalhar aspectos metodológicos das pesquisas registradas”, escreveu Nunes Marques na decisão.

Algumas das novas exigências na hora do registro incluem:

descrição da amostra da pesquisa, descrevendo a população que foi entrevistada, o nível de confiança e margem de erro máxima;

detalhamento da metodologia de campo, com a base utilizada para acessar o eleitorado e a indicação o uso de mídias durante a entrevista;

exigência sobre a estrutura do questionário, com informações sobre a ordem das perguntas que foi apresentada aos entrevistados.

Além disso, para depois da divulgação das pesquisas, as empresas devem:

registrar o dia e a hora do início e do fim da realização dos questionários;

apresentar a amostra real e o descarte, mostrando o tamanho efetivo da amostra e se houve alguma recusa, perda ou substituição de entrevistados;

demonstrar o modo de coleta das respostas, incluindo a plataforma utilizada, metodologia de ponderação e medidas de precisão estatística;

trazer o cálculo da taxa de resposta e identificar eventuais limitações metodológicas em um relatório próprio.

Para a Associação Brasileira de Empresas de Pesquisa (Abep), a “preocupação” é com “o momento, a forma e o procedimento adotados para a introdução das novas exigências”. Em nota à imprensa, a entidade, que representa ao menos 104 empresas do setor, critica o fato de as novas regras passarem a valer durante o processo eleitoral.

“O artigo 105 da Lei nº 9.504/1997 estabelece prazo e procedimento próprios para a edição das instruções destinadas às eleições, refletindo a necessidade de previsibilidade e segurança jurídica das regras aplicáveis ao pleito”, afirma a Abep (leia a íntegra da nota ao final desta reportagem).

A Abep reúne empresas de pesquisas de mercado, opinião e mídia e atua na promoção de padrões de qualidade e boas práticas no setor.

No posicionamento, a associação também afirma que os novos campos obrigatórios não foram submetidos a debate público antes de sua adoção. No ofício, por sua vez, o presidente do TSE afirmou que a medida resultou de estudos de um grupo de trabalho criado pela corte a partir de sugestões de representantes das empresas.

“O Grupo de Trabalho instituído pelo TSE reúne profissionais de reconhecida qualificação acadêmica e técnica, cuja contribuição é relevante. Entretanto, o conhecimento teórico precisa ser complementado pela experiência prática das empresas que executam pesquisas em diferentes regiões, com distintos desenhos amostrais, modos de coleta, sistemas, equipes e condições de campo”, diz a Abep.

A associação ainda tratou das informações dos levantamentos que se tornarão públicos. Segundo a Abep, é importante definir quais informações serão públicas, em que momento e com qual finalidade, “preservando o equilíbrio entre fiscalização e proteção legítima do conhecimento técnico desenvolvido pelos institutos”.

Por fim, a Abep defende que a implementação das mudanças deveria ocorrer somente depois de um debate técnico mais amplo com participação efetiva do setor e em “período adequado de transição”.

O anúncio do presidente do TSE e a nota foram divulgadas dois meses depois que o ministro propôs criar um selo para reconhecer os institutos cujas pesquisas mais se aproximassem dos resultados oficiais das urnas . A proposta foi apresentada pelo presidente durante reunião com representantes do setor, sem aviso prévio. Ministros do TSE ouvidos pelo g1 também disseram que foram pegos de surpresa a respeito do tema da reunião. Eles descreveram a proposta como "constrangedora".

Depois do encontro, a entidade publicou uma nota na qual afirmou que a iniciativa parte de uma compreensão equivocada sobre a finalidade das pesquisas eleitorais. Segundo a associação, os levantamentos medem a intenção de voto no momento em que são realizados e não representam previsões ou promessas de resultado. “ Exigir que uma pesquisa ‘acerte’ o resultado é confundir ciência com bola de cristal”, afirmou a ABEP . Em minoria, Nunes Marques recuou a respeito da ideia de implementar o selo de acurácia.

Leia a íntegra do posicionamento da Abep:

A Associação Brasileira de Empresas de Pesquisa (ABEP) reconhece o relevante trabalho desenvolvido pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral para ampliar a transparência, a fiscalização e a qualidade das informações relacionadas às pesquisas eleitorais. O Sistema de Registro das Pesquisas Eleitorais (PesqEle) é instrumento importante para a sociedade e para o acompanhamento do processo eleitoral, e seu permanente aperfeiçoamento é objetivo também compartilhado pelo setor.

A preocupação da ABEP com as alterações recentemente anunciadas não está, portanto, na finalidade da medida, mas no momento, na forma e no procedimento adotados para a introdução das novas exigências.

A partir de 5 de outubro de 2026, as empresas passarão a prestar informações significativamente mais detalhadas sobre desenho amostral, procedimentos de seleção, bases utilizadas, fórmulas de cálculo, ponderação, modos de coleta, taxas de resposta e limitações metodológicas.

Embora parte dessas informações esteja relacionada a obrigações já previstas na regulamentação eleitoral, o nível de detalhamento agora exigido representa, na prática, uma ampliação relevante do conteúdo atualmente prestado no registro das pesquisas e demanda adaptações técnicas e operacionais por parte dos institutos.

A ABEP entende que alterações dessa extensão deveriam ser precedidas de discussão técnica específica, participação efetiva das empresas e entidades representativas do setor e prazo adequado para testes e adaptação.

Essa preocupação é ainda maior porque as novas exigências serão implementadas durante o próprio processo eleitoral. O artigo 105 da Lei nº 9.504/1997 estabelece prazo e procedimento próprios para a edição das instruções destinadas às eleições, refletindo a necessidade de previsibilidade e segurança jurídica das regras aplicáveis ao pleito.

O Grupo de Trabalho instituído pelo TSE reúne profissionais de reconhecida qualificação acadêmica e técnica, cuja contribuição é relevante. Entretanto, o conhecimento teórico precisa ser complementado pela experiência prática das empresas que executam pesquisas em diferentes regiões, com distintos desenhos amostrais, modos de coleta, sistemas, equipes e condições de campo.

Embora representantes do setor tenham participado de reuniões anteriores com o Tribunal, as empresas e suas entidades representativas não integram formalmente o Grupo de Trabalho, e o conjunto específico dos novos campos não foi submetido a debate público próprio antes da definição de sua obrigatoriedade.

Outro aspecto que precisa ser esclarecido é a publicidade das novas informações. A ABEP apoia a transparência do PesqEle, mas alguns dos dados solicitados alcançam procedimentos metodológicos bastante detalhados.

É importante definir quais informações serão públicas, em que momento e com qual finalidade, preservando o equilíbrio entre fiscalização e proteção legítima do conhecimento técnico desenvolvido pelos institutos.

Também é necessário estabelecer critérios claros para o preenchimento e a interpretação dos novos campos. A pesquisa eleitoral utiliza diferentes metodologias, todas sujeitas a particularidades técnicas. Divergências metodológicas legítimas não podem ser transformadas em irregularidades simplesmente porque determinado método não se ajusta perfeitamente a uma classificação padronizada pelo sistema.

Por essas razões, a ABEP considera inadequada a aplicação obrigatória das novas exigências ainda nas Eleições de 2026 e entende que sua implementação deveria ser precedida de debate técnico mais amplo, participação efetiva do setor e período adequado de transição.

A ABEP permanece à disposição do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral para contribuir com esse processo, buscando conciliar transparência, fiscalização, segurança jurídica, diversidade metodológica e as condições práticas necessárias à adequada realização das pesquisas eleitorais.

articles.title: Proibição das bets: Justiça vai fiscalizar loterias estaduais | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministério da Justiça divulgou nesta segunda (29) o balanço de ações contra as bets nos primeiros dias de vigência da MP que proíbe as bets no país, assinada pelo presidente Lula.
articles.summary: O Ministério da Justiça fiscaliza se loterias estaduais cumprem a proibição das bets após o governo federal solicitar o bloqueio de mais de 5 mil sites.
articles.body:
O Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública se prepara para fiscalizar se loterias estaduais em nove estados do Brasil estão seguindo as regras da Medida Provisória (MP) do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) que proibiu a operação das bets no Brasil.

O assunto vai ser abordado em uma portaria, que ainda não tem texto pronto. Entre os estados que devem ter suas loterias fiscalizadas estão:

Segundo o governo, já foram encaminhados pedidos para bloqueio de 5.209 sites de apostas por meio da atuação da Anatel e do Comitê Gestor da Internet no Brasil.

A Anatel acionou uma rede de mais de 21 mil prestadoras de internet em todo o território nacional para efetivar a derrubada imediata dos domínios

Além disso, houve a notificação para remoção, até 6 de outubro, de 186 aplicativos disponíveis nas lojas da Apple e do Google.

O balanço também detalhou medidas em relação à publicidade e à atuação em redes sociais e plataformas digitais entre os dias 27 e 29 de setembro:

Facebook e Instagram: foram solicitadas as remoções de 300 páginas no Facebook e 90 perfis no Instagram.

Telegram: ações de monitoramento alcançaram mais de um milhão de membros e usuários de canais, grupos e perfis de bets ilegais.

Outras plataformas de tecnologia: oito grandes plataformas (Google, Meta, YouTube, X, Telegram, TikTok, Kwai e Discord) foram notificadas pela Secretaria de Direitos Digitais para retirar propagandas irregulares no prazo de dez dias.

Governo anuncia proibição das bets no Brasil 3 anos após ter regulamentado as empresas de apostas — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

🔎 Às vésperas do primeiro turno das eleições, o presidente Lula, que é candidato à reeleição, anunciou a proibição total de apostas de quota fixa no país, as chamadas bets. A vedação inclui também jogos online e cassinos virtuais no país, como por exemplo, o "Jogo do Tigrinho".

🔎 Lula também enviou ao Congresso Nacional um projeto de lei que estabelece penas para quem explorar, operar ou divulgar as bets e os cassinos virtuais. Ao tomar as medidas, o petista mencionou o endividamento de famílias e o vício de apostadores em jogos de azar.

"Agora, todas as bets passam a ser ilegais. Ninguém pode oferecer o jogo. Isso [o combate] está sendo feito com mecanismos tanto da Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas como do Ministério da Justiça, através do Cyberlab, utilizando ferramentas tecnológicas. Como a oferta do jogo é feita no ambiente virtual, a gente tem uma série de mecanismos que identificam esses sites", afirmou o secretário nacional de segurança, Chico Lucas.

O governo também iniciou processos administrativos contra empresas de apostas flagradas em irregularidades. A medida decorre de 63 registros encaminhados pela Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas.

Paralelamente, o Banco Central foi acionado para rastrear a cadeia de pagamentos.

Os recursos e bens que serão retirados das bets ilegais serão revertidos para o Fundo Nacional de Segurança Pública.

A estratégia do governo federal busca asfixiar o ecossistema do jogo ilegal em duas frentes simultâneas:

o combate direto à atividade criminosa na internet; e

a interrupção da divulgação e propagação dessas plataformas junto à população brasileira.

Desde sexta-feira passada, os sites de apostas estão proibidos de receber novos depósitos. Os usuários poderão apenas resgatar os saldos de suas contas, prazo que se encerra às 23h59 do dia 5 de outubro.

No dia seguinte, 6 de outubro, todos os sites e aplicativos de apostas sairão definitivamente do ar. Entre os dias 7 e 8 de outubro, as empresas vão apurar o saldo restante de cada apostador (atrelado ao CPF) e enviar esses dados aos bancos. Por fim, a partir de 9 de outubro, as instituições financeiras iniciarão a devolução integral desses valores aos respectivos donos.

O governo alertou que as plataformas banidas não oferecem nenhuma garantia de recebimento de prêmios ou devolução de valores. E destacaram que constataram práticas abusivas, como propagandas enganosas que tratavam o jogo como investimento e mecanismos que induziam o apostador a gastar cada vez mais dinheiro.

"Hoje no Brasil, essa garantia ela não existe. É um alerta e é importante que ele [o apostador] tenha essa informação, porque é esse consumidor a partir dessa decisão que vai poder proteger o seu patrimônio e a sua saúde", destacou o secretário nacional do consumidor, Ricardo Morishita.

articles.title: Mendonça libera post de Erika Hilton sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro André Mendonça entendeu que postagem da deputada do PSOL não reproduzia o conteúdo considerado "notoriamente inverídico" em decisão anterior.
articles.summary: Ministro André Mendonça entendeu que postagem da deputada do PSOL não reproduzia o conteúdo considerado "notoriamente inverídico" em decisão anterior.
articles.body:
O ministro André Mendonça, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), reconsiderou parte de uma decisão e liberou uma publicação da deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) sobre uma possível mudança no status de Nossa Senhora Aparecida como padroeira do Brasil.

A postagem havia sido incluída em um conjunto de conteúdos retirados do ar por determinação de Mendonça, em decisão tomada após pedido da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Ao analisar um recurso apresentado pela parlamentar, o ministro decidiu restabelecer a publicação.

Na nova decisão, Mendonça afirmou que o conteúdo divulgado por Erika Hilton "não reproduz o núcleo factual considerado notoriamente inverídico" que embasou a ordem anterior de remoção.

No texto, a deputada criticava um projeto de lei apresentado em 2007 e arquivado no ano seguinte. A proposta previa que Nossa Senhora Aparecida fosse reconhecida como padroeira "dos brasileiros católicos apostólicos romanos", e não mais como padroeira "do Brasil".

"Repudio, com veemência, o Projeto de Lei que retira o título de Padroeira do Brasil de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, apresentado na Câmara por Victório Galli Filho, ex-assessor especial da Presidência da República de Jair Bolsonaro. Cresci em lar evangélico, não sou católica, defendo o estado laico e, mesmo assim, considero essa proposta esdrúxula", afirma Hilton na publicação.

"E, apesar de a proposta ser de 2007 e já ter sido arquivada, qualquer movimento que sugira que ela pode retornar ao debate público pelas mãos de Flávio Bolsonaro, que quer ser presidente do Brasil, ou pelas mãos de seus aliados políticos, precisa ser observado com cautela e atenção", conclui a parlamentar.

Segundo o ministro, a publicação fazia referência a um projeto que efetivamente tramitou no Congresso Nacional, o que a diferencia das demais postagens que permaneceram alcançadas pela decisão de remoção.

Deputada Erika Hilton (PSOL) — Foto: Zeca Ribeiro/Câmara dos Deputados Fonte: Agência Câmara de Notícias

A controvérsia começou após a circulação, nas redes sociais, de publicações que associavam Flávio Bolsonaro e setores da direita a uma suposta iniciativa para retirar de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil. O candidato negou a existência de qualquer proposta nesse sentido.

Na sexta-feira (25), Mendonça determinou a remoção de publicações relacionadas ao tema, entendendo que a narrativa não encontrava suporte na realidade e já havia sido corrigida publicamente. A decisão também autorizou que plataformas removessem réplicas do mesmo conteúdo considerado desinformativo.

No domingo (27), Dino derrubou essa ordem ao atender a um pedido apresentado por Tabet.

Nesta segunda (28), a defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro recorreu ao STF e pediu a suspensão da decisão.

Horas depois, Fux acolheu o pedido e restabeleceu os efeitos das determinações do TSE até que o plenário do Supremo analise o tema.

Tanto Dino quanto Fux defenderam que o caso seja analisado pelo plenário da Corte. Até o momento, porém, não há data prevista para o julgamento.

Ministro André Mendonça em sessão do STF sobre caso Master - 15/09/2026 — Foto: Alejandro Zambrana/STF

articles.title: Kassio Nunes Marques marca julgamento virtual do TSE sobre os posts de Nossa Senhora Aparecida  | G1
articles.standfirst: Na segunda-feira (28), o ministro Luiz Fux, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), suspendeu a decisão do ministro Flávio Dino que, por sua vez, havia derrubado uma ordem do ministro André Mendonça.
articles.summary: Na segunda-feira (28), o ministro Luiz Fux, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), suspendeu a decisão do ministro Flávio Dino que, por sua vez, havia derrubado uma ordem do ministro André Mendonça.
articles.body:
O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, marcou para esta quarta-feira (30) uma sessão do plenário virtual da Corte Eleitoral para analisar a decisão do ministro André Mendonça que removeu as publicações que associavam o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a um suposto movimento de retirada de Nossa Senhora Aparecida do posto de padroeira do Brasil.

Com a decisão, Fux restabeleceu, até a análise pelo plenário do STF , a determinação de Mendonça para retirar do ar as postagens, que incluíam a uma publicação do humorista Antonio Tabet.

A decisão de Dino, tomada no domingo (27), havia permitido o restabelecimento do post de Tabet e de outras publicações removidas pelo mesmo fundamento.

Dino argumentou que a postagem não citava nominalmente Flávio Bolsonaro e que a medida era necessária para proteger a liberdade de expressão.

Nunes Marques em sessão plenária do TSE — Foto: Antonio Augusto/TSE

Fux, que atendeu a um pedido da defesa do candidato, defendeu que o tema fosse examinado pelo colegiado diante dos impactos sobre a Justiça Eleitoral e sobre a disputa presidencial em curso.

O presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin, chegou a sinalizar que pautaria o assunto nesta quarta-feira (30), o que não chegou a ser confirmado.

"Eu tenho a convicção de que tentaram matar o meu pai porque viram que ele já era presidente do Brasil em 2018. Por isso, foram para tentar eliminá-lo. Foi aquela facada, lá em Juiz de Fora... Para você ver, mais uma vez. Eu acho que eu posso considerar uma espécie de facada essa fake news em mim", disse o candidato ao SantoFlow Podcast.

"Enquanto eu for presidente da República, ninguém vai avacalhar com Nossa Senhora Aparecida. Ninguém. As pessoas precisam aprender a respeitar todas as religiões, inclusive as religiões de matriz africana. É preciso. Ninguém é dono da verdade. A única igreja mentirosa é aquela da Lagoinha, daquele pastor chamado Valadão, que era sócio do Vorcaro", afirmou Lula.

A Igreja Batista da Lagoinha tem sede em Belo Horizonte, em Minas Gerais, e recebeu repasses por investigados ligados ao ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, segundo relatórios do Conselho de Controle de Atividades Financeiras (Coaf).

Perto de completar um mês, a crise institucional vivida pelo STF provoca impactos no TSE, na reta final do primeiro turno.

A ala alinhada ao ministro André Mendonça chegou a procurar o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, na segunda para questionar ações de aliados do ministro Alexandre de Moraes que, na avaliação desses integrantes da Corte, tentam arrastar a Corte Eleitoral.

A tentativa desse grupo de ministros era acelerar o julgamento no plenário da decisão de Dino que derrubou a ordem de Mendonça, tomada no TSE, para que plataformas excluíssem postagens sobre a discussão em torno do título de padroeira de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

Em outra frente, os aliados de Moraes indicavam que uma discussão na véspera da eleição poderia expor ainda mais o tribunal e acirrar a erosão interna na cúpula do Judiciário.

articles.title: PF investiga Willer Tomaz por suposta lavagem de dinheiro em casa de apostas; em 18 meses, advogado apostou R$ 6,6 bilhões | G1
articles.standfirst: No período, advogado depositou R$ 325 milhões em uma única bet. Valores eram reaplicados até que movimentação atingisse a casa dos bilhões.
articles.summary: No período, advogado depositou R$ 325 milhões em uma única bet. Valores eram reaplicados até que movimentação atingisse a casa dos bilhões.
articles.body:
Comissão Parlamentar Mista de Inquérito (CPMI) da JBS realiza reunião para oitiva do advogado Willer Tomaz e apreciação de requerimentos. — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

A Polícia Federal (PF) investiga se Willer Tomaz de Sousa usou operações de apostas para lavar de dinheiro. Ao todo, em 18 meses (de janeiro de 2025 a julho de 2026), o advogado apostou R$ 6,6 bilhões e teve um prejuízo de R$ 188,5 milhões.

Os dados foram informados pela defesa do advogado em um processo aberto contra a casa de apostas Blaze, que patrocina o atacante do Santos, Neymar Jr, e que tinha contrato com a influenciadora, Virgínia Fonseca.

O processo foi protocolado em agosto deste ano e estava em sigilo até o começo da tarde desta terça-feira (29).

A informação foi inicialmente publicada pelo Metrópoles. O g1 teve acesso ao processo.

No pedido, a defesa disse que Tomaz foi diagnosticado com o transtorno mental caracterizado pela perda de controle sobre o impulso de jogar e apostar, a ludopatia - e pediu a restituição de todos os valores enviados à Blaze.

"O autor é, portanto, pessoa diagnosticada com ludopatia por laudo de profissional de saúde mental habilitado", justificou a defesa.

Em uma das respostas ao processo, a casa de apostas discordou com a denominação de prejuízo das operações usado pela defesa de Tomaz, justificando que "não é dano".

"O movimento líquido da conta não é dano. Ele é a diferença entre o que entrou e o que saiu de uma conta que funcionou, ao longo de dezoito meses, como conta corrente, com entradas e saídas sucessivas, muitas vezes no mesmo dia. Somar depósitos e chamar o resultado de prejuízo equivale a somar apenas os débitos de um extrato bancário, ignorando os créditos", justificou a casa de apostas.

Ainda de acordo com os dados informados pela defesa, no período de 18 meses, entre 2025 e 2026, Tomaz realizou 2.145 depósitos na casa de aposta, totalizando R$ 325 milhões .

Com esse dinheiro, ele realizava sucessivas apostas até atingir a quantia bilionária movimentada.

Esse valor, segundo a defesa, pode ser maior. Os advogados argumentam que não conseguiram acessar os dados de jogos anteriores a 2025 e que já verificaram a existência de 55 páginas de depósitos nos registros anteriores a essa data.

Ainda de acordo com a defesa, a principal causa das perdas de Tomaz foram as mesas de cassino online, que admitiam apostas de até R$ 500 mil em rodadas que duravam 30 segundos.

"A ciência existiu e está documentada em mais de uma via: o autor comunicou expressamente o diagnóstico de ludopatia aos atendentes da ré, em pelo menos duas sessões distintas de atendimento, pediu em três protocolos formais o bloqueio definitivo de sua conta e, dirigiu à ré, pelo canal do próprio gerente de contas por ela designado, notificação pré-litigiosa circunstanciada — cujo recebimento a ré confirmou formalmente, subscrevendo-se 'Blaze Team' e anunciando 'structured internal review'".

A defesa também critica a estrutura organizacional da casa de apostas, que permite o depósito de até R$ 500 mil de uma só vez, mas limita os saques a R$ 100 mil por operação.

"Forçado pelo teto, o autor fracionou a retirada: 16 saques de R$ 100.000,00 — R$ 1.600.000,00 — solicitados entre 00h19 e 00h25. [...] Ao tentar sacar os R$ 100.000,00 restantes do saldo, o autor foi bloqueado pelo próprio sistema: 'Você fez muitas tentativas consecutivas. Por favor, tente novamente mais tarde".

Com isso, apenas em uma noite, o advogado aplicou R$ 1,9 milhão, restando apenas R$ 0,29 na conta, após sucessivas perdas.

Em abril de 2023, quando as casas de apostas ainda não estavam regularizadas no Brasil, a Blaze criou um grupo no Whatsapp para atendimento exclusivo ao advogado.

As mesas de cassino, principais opções de jogos dele, inicialmente tinham uma limitação bem menor para apostas do que o patamar de R$ 500 mil registrada ao final.

A princípio, as apostas máximas eram limitadas a R$ 125 mil e foram aumentando de acordo com pedidos feitos por Tomaz.

A defesa aponta ainda que, ao longo do período, a casa de apostas ofereceu R$ 42,2 milhões em "estímulos" a Tomaz, que eram uma espécie de bônus pela assiduidade do advogado.

Willer Tomaz é investigado pela PF no âmbito da Operação Sem Desconto, que revelou descontos associativos não autorizados em aposentadorias e pensões do INSS .

A fase da operação que teve Tomaz como um dos alvos investigava um esquema de lavagem de dinheiro que teria beneficiado o senador Weverton Rocha (PDT).

A PF descreveu Tomaz como uma espécie de estrutura de sustentação financeira e patrimonial a Weverton, envolvendo empresas, imóveis, aeronaves e outros operadores.

Tomaz chegou a ser preso em 2017, suspeito de tentar interferir nas investigações da Operação Greenfield, que apurou fraudes em fundos de pensão.

articles.title: Democrats are running pastors for office. Republicans are attacking their religious comments.
articles.summary: Democratic Senate nominees James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as two key Iowa House nominees, are seeing their remarks on Christian...
articles.body:
A slate of Democrats are running for Congress leaning on their Christian bona fides. Republicans are trying to portray them as wolves in sheep's clothing.

In Texas, Republicans are running ads blasting seminarian James Talarico for saying he's "a Christian who hates Christianity." In Iowa, they are going after a pair of clergy in key House races as "PINOS" — "pastors in name only," because they "don't profess the true gospel of Jesus Christ." In Kansas, Republicans pan megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton as "too woke and too weak."

"His sermons are essentially a carbon copy of the Democrat National Committee platform," said Brent Robertson, chief of staff to Hamilton's opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), pointing to a past sermon in which Hamilton urged followers to reduce their carbon footprint .

The closing arguments on these Democrats — as evidenced by the most recent ads — shows a concerted effort to turn their preaching against them to paint them as fake, corrupt or even blasphemous .

In Texas, MAGA Inc. is on air painting Talarico as a "liberal weirdo," clipping Talarico's controversial statements, like "Jesus Christ Himself was a radical feminist" and "God is non-binary."

The Trump-aligned No Going Back PAC is on air in Iowa's 2nd District hitting Presbyterian minister and Democrat Lindsay James as inauthentic: "When the cameras are on, Lindsay James goes into a character, a caring pastor who says what you want to hear, but when there's no spotlight, Lindsay James shows just how radical she can be."

And in Kansas, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign is on air slamming Hamilton as a "slimy," "millionaire megachurch CEO," saying he "used faith to fatten his wallet" and "asked churchgoers to pony up for God, then use church resources for his own campaign."

"The swamp's got enough money changers," the ad says.

The attacks are coming precisely because these candidates have proven to be formidable candidates in purple to red areas, using their faith backgrounds to bolster themselves against GOP accusations that they're out of their state's mainstream. Talarico poses Democrats' best chance to flip a Texas Senate seat in nearly four decades. Hamilton has turned deep-red Kansas into a battleground. And James and Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, are running tough in a pair of Iowa districts Trump won in 2024.

Voters "understand and appreciate authenticity, and they know that faith without works is dead," said Chaz Molder, the Democratic nominee in Tennessee's deep-red 2nd District who leads a Sunday School class with his wife. "And just posting scripture on Sunday morning to point out that they went to church is not enough."

But with Democrats' clerical credibility comes a practical challenge: years and years of on-camera sermons, a treasure trove for oppo researchers. It's become a challenge in Hamilton's race, where Vice President JD Vance joined the pile-on earlier this month: During a visit to Iowa, he took a shot at Hamilton as having "kind of a 'gee whiz, I'm a nice pastor' vibe," but said he "tells his congregation not about the gospel of Jesus Christ, but that they need to repent for their white privilege while eating beef."

Democrats have largely brushed off the attacks. Talarico has said he's "missed the mark" on some of his "cringey" past comments but has doubled down on his sermonizing: "When I take on the politicians who are serving themselves and not the people, I'm doing it on biblical grounds," he said in a sermon last weekend. A James spokesperson criticized Republicans for "desperately attacking Lindsay's deeply held faith commitments. If it wasn't so insulting to other Iowa Christians, it would be laughable." Hamilton has seen clergy run to his side: 120 fellow Methodist ministers across Kansas wrote an open letter to Marshall telling him to stop attacking Hamilton's pastoral ministry, saying the attacks "tear at the fabric that is the body of Christ."

"We're not the first Christians to be attacked for our faith, and we won't let smears and lies from a couple of Washington politicians stop us from living out our values in the world," Hamilton said in a video after Vance's speech.

In many ways, this election marks something of a faith resurgence for the Democratic Party. While only half of Democrat- and Democrat-leaning U.S. adults identify as Christian (a 24-percentage-point decline since 2007), Democrats this cycle are running clergy, Sunday School teachers, chaplains and other devout Christians across the map.

"As a person of faith, I think that it's time for the Democratic Party to reassert that Democrats are a big tent, and we have many elected officials from different faiths for whom faith is something very important to them," said Ben McAdams, the Democratic nominee in Utah's 1st District and a volunteer Sunday School teacher in his Latter-day Saint congregation in Salt Lake City. "The Republican Party of Donald Trump does not seem to be reflecting the Christian values that I grew up with."

Doug Pagitt, executive director of progressive group Vote Common Good, counts nine clergy running for federal office this cycle as Democrats — something he hasn't seen before.

"The idea that a faith leader, especially a white faith leader, would run as a Democrat and be forthright about it … it's really unusual," Pagitt said. "We've had candidates [in the past] whose moms were pastors, and they were nervous about mentioning that in the Democratic Party circles. But that seems to have shifted and changed."

articles.title: Soros nephew divulges how family's power helped bankroll El-Sayed's education during secretive fundraiser
articles.summary: Jeffrey Soros revealed his role in launching Abdul El-Sayed's career at a secretive Hollywood fundraiser where attendees were asked not to record.
articles.body:
Jeffrey Soros, the nephew of billionaire Democrat mega-donor George Soros, hosted a fundraiser for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, revealing his long-standing connection to the candidate.

Soros disclosed that he played a key role in helping El-Sayed kickstart his career, mentioning their association since 2012 and highlighting El-Sayed's past as a recipient of the Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans.

The fundraiser, attended by Hollywood notables, allowed donations of up to $57,800 to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, with the Soros family's political machine also contributing millions to support El-Sayed's Senate campaign.

FIRST ON FOX: Jeffrey Soros, the wealthy nephew of billionaire Democrat mega-donor George Soros, detailed his yearslong connection to Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during a Monday night fundraiser, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital.

The Soros nephew, a wealthy Hollywood producer, hosted El-Sayed at his home Monday night for a fundraiser that attracted controversy given the emphasis the candidate has placed on getting money out of politics. During remarks, Soros noted that he played a key role in helping El-Sayed get his career off the ground, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital.

"I just wanted to welcome you here and express my appreciation for coming. And it's been a privilege," Soros said while standing next to El-Sayed during the event, the footage showed. "Speaking of privilege, I've had the pleasure of knowing Abdul since 2012. I got to interview him as a finalist for my parents. Fellowship, the Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans."

The El-Sayed campaign and the Los Angeles Media Fund, where Soros serves as CEO, did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Attendees were asked not to record the event, a common practice at many political fundraisers, organizers said in footage reviewed by Fox News Digital.

The Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans, which is designed to help immigrants and the children of immigrants get a leg up in the United States, pays out tens of thousands of dollars in stipend and tuition support to winners. El-Sayed won the fellowship in 2012, and it is touted on its website as one of its success stories.

The financial and political ties come as El-Sayed has made the influence of wealthy donors a recurring theme of his campaign.

"The fundamental corruption of our politics has been the system that allows corporations and would-be oligarchs and billionaires to buy politicians," El-Sayed said during a 2025 local news interview.

"I want to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for All ," he said during a follow-up interview.

A flyer promoting the Soros fundraiser , which was attended by Hollywood notables, stated that attendees could donate up to $57,800 to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, Fox News Digital previously reported. The Soros family's political machine has also dumped millions into political committees that are supporting El-Sayed's run for Senate.

"Abdul El-Sayed raising dark Soros money in California after begging Chuck Schumer for money in DC is the least surprising thing he's done all cycle," Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for GOP nominee Mike Rogers' campaign, previously told Fox News Digital. "That's what a conman does — says one thing and does another. Michiganders can't trust this guy."

El-Sayed's campaign has defended itself by arguing that "corporate special interests are spending millions of dollars in dark money to try to buy Rogers a Senate seat because he's spent his entire career making himself and his billionaire donors richer while Michiganders pay the price."

articles.title: GOP senator blocks effort to bar Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center
articles.summary: Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee blocked a bipartisan effort to prevent President Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center.
articles.body:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president. An objection from a single senator can block a bill from being passed by unanimous consent.

The bill – dubbed the "Protecting Presidential Memorials Act" – would also apply to Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument. But Merkley and Murkowski made their immediate goal clear.

"This has of course to do with the president planning to demolish the Kennedy Center," Merkley said on the Senate floor late Monday evening, Sept. 28, after the passing of the Protect College Sports Act , a major overhaul to college athletics related to NIL (name, image and likeliness) payment for student athletes.

Lee's office said in a statement to USA TODAY that this effort should go through "the appropriate committee process."

"Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate's time with partisan scaremongering," Lee said in the statement shared by communications director Billy Gribbin.

Trump's naming campaign, from the Kennedy Center to Trump RX

From Lake America to buildings and institutions bearing Trump's name, see the places, landmarks and public spaces tied to the president's branding campaign. Pictured here, a map labeling Lake Ontario as " Lake America " is displayed as President Donald Trump signs an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" on Aug. 27, 2026, amid an ongoing trade war between the U.S. and Canada. See what Trump has renamed or attached his name to.

The Senate vote is the latest chapter in a year of legal wrangling and congressional wrangling over the Kennedy Center.

The Kennedy Center added Trump's name to the building's facade in December 2025 after the board – which was handpicked by Trump – voted to rename the center. In June 2026, a judge ordered that his name be taken down, saying that an act of Congress was needed to change the name of the memorial to the assassinated president.

Trump's name has since been removed , but a tarp remains covering the building's name where Trump's name used to be.

Earlier in September, the Kennedy Center closed after part of the ceiling collapsed , and on Sept. 15 the center's board voted to close the center for two years.

That came after a federal judge's second ruling that Trump's name could not be added to the building in September 2026, the culmination of months of legal disputes as the president contended that the center needed to be renovated, that only he could raise the money for it and that his administration should be recognized for it.

Trump has continued to defend his stance about his name being on the building, saying on Sept. 18 that the center had "been a dump" and "lost money" for years. He said that he would subsidize the necessary repairs but said that his administration should be recognized.

Merkley accused the president of wanting to demolish the center, pointing to an i mage captured of Trump inside Air Force One reading a poster that appears to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." The photo was taken hours after Trump told reporters that the memorial will "end up being ripped down" unless major renovations are undertaken.

articles.title: Supreme Court lets Trump resume deporting migrants to countries not their own
articles.summary: Sept 29 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own w...
articles.body:
Sept 29 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.

The court granted ‌the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to so-called third ‌countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on the policy to follow.

The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision to let ​the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of the litigation.

Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.

More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.

The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced ‌a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning ⁠to office last year.

The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.

Department of Homeland Security General ⁠Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.

"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an ​opportunity ​to raise a fear claim."

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process ​protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government ‌to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.

The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.

The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.

The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. ‌For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities ​would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In its emergency ​filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to ​remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."

But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had ‌been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.

The ​policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by ​third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.

The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution ​or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.

The Boston-based 1st US Circuit ‌Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly ​violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send ​a group of migrants to South Sudan.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title: Republicans wanted Jack Smith to give them a smoking gun. They got a gaffe instead.
articles.summary: The former special counsel’s appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee was marked by personal insults rather than new revelations.
articles.body:
It started with a pledge to expose a Biden-era conspiracy to take down President Donald Trump. It ended with a botched attack over basketball tickets.

Armed with subpoena power in Congress and a friendly Justice Department on their side, Republican lawmakers have spent two years promising to expose former special counsel Jack Smith as the leader of an anti-Trump witch hunt that morphed into a full-blown attempt to take down the Republican establishment.

Smith's appearance Tuesday before the Senate Judiciary Committee — his third time testifying under oath on Capitol Hill, the second time in public — was supposed to be a watershed moment for the GOP intent on extracting a smoking gun ahead of the midterm elections. Instead, the hearing was most memorable for the fusillade of insults hurled by the panel's Republicans.

Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri unsuccessfully sought to implicate Smith in a plot to attend a sporting event as a cover for investigating Trump election interference claims, then called him a "dirtbag." Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said the former prosecutor made him "want to throw up in my mouth." And Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, comparing him to "Javert from 'Les Mis,'" said Smith's probe was "the most egregious abuse of power in the history of the Department of Justice."

Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley insisted the hearing was "not the end" of his investigative work, but the four-hour grilling had the feeling of finality. The Republican-led probe into Smith's efforts to bring criminal charges against the president has already stretched for two years, and Democrats stand a chance of retaking control of Congress in the midterms.

And at least one Republican member of the panel, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, said he believed the investigation into Smith had run its course in Congress.

"At this point, I think we kind of know what we know," Hawley said in an interview following the hearing. "I think at this point, it's up to the DOJ to either prosecute him for perjury for lying under oath, which I think the House has formally referred him for … or try to have him disbarred."

Judiciary Committee Republicans did little Tuesday to challenge the substance of Smith's criminal case against Trump for seeking to subvert the 2020 presidential election. Smith reinforced his contention that Trump mounted an unprecedented criminal assault on the transfer of power, seeking to derail Joe Biden's victory and then capitalizing on the Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the Capitol — unleashed by a mob of his supporters — to further that goal.

Smith also defended the work of his staff and decried the Trump-led Justice Department's decision to fire them as "illegal." And he made his most forceful case yet that the probe he led was actually fueled by Republican witnesses who broke from Trump over his handling of the 2020 election.

"It's very hard to understand how our investigation can be viewed as partisan when the strongest witnesses, the people who were the difference between the rule of law and not, were Republicans," Smith said.

When Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ripped into Smith for secretly obtaining her late brother Lindsey Graham's phone records as part of his inquiry, Smith hailed him as a "patriotic public servant" and who likely would have been a featured witness in Trump's trial — because he eventually concluded Trump's election fraud claims were false.

Smith similarly hailed Former Arizona House Speaker Rusty Bowers and former Vice President Mike Pence as heroic figures who were crucial witnesses against the president. Smith ultimately dropped his case after Trump prevailed in the 2024 election. Though he said he remained confident in his ability to secure a conviction at trial, Smith emphasized that Justice Department policy forbids criminal prosecution of a sitting president.

When they weren't lobbing personal attacks at Smith, Republicans homed in on what they described as procedural flaws of Smith's investigation. They criticized him for subpoenaing phone records of members of Congress, like Lindsey Graham, who communicated with Trump and his administration during the post-2020 election timeframe.

They hit Smith for securing court orders that prevented telecom companies from alerting lawmakers to those subpoenas, and challenged his respect for the constitutional protections members of Congress are afforded to avoid scrutiny from federal prosecutors. That line of questioning produced one of the only bipartisan moments of the hearing: a pitch by Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah) for legislation that would limit the ability of prosecutors to obtain secrecy orders when they issue subpoenas in sensitive probes.

Lee is poised to be the next chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee in the next Congress if Republicans maintain control of the chamber.

Smith used his appearance, as well as friendly questions from the panel's Democrats, to parry GOP criticism of his tactics. He followed all Justice Department policies and laws, he insisted, and said he had respect for the separation of powers — including Congress' constitutional protection from executive branch scrutiny.

Smith said he never targeted GOP lawmakers but pursued critical evidence of Trump's actions and state of mind that would have been necessary to prove his case in court, and he repeatedly returned to an overarching contention: that he had enough evidence to convict Trump of "one of the most serious crimes that's ever happened in our nation's history."

He also reminded lawmakers what he couldn't say: anything at all about his charges against Trump for hoarding classified information at Mar-a-Lago. Smith's findings in that probe remain sealed from public view by U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, who has ordered the Justice Department to keep it secret.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) said subpoenaing that report would be one of Democrats' first actions should they have the majority in the next Congress.

Ultimately, Smith's hearing Tuesday may end up being best remembered for a high-profile gaffe by Schmitt, who accused Smith of secretly traveling to Atlanta at the very moment local prosecutor Fani Willis — who had also charged Trump over the 2020 election scheme — was facing damaging questions about her conduct. As proof, displayed on an elaborate poster, Schmitt offered text messages suggesting that Smith attended a basketball game on Feb. 3, 2024 — the same day the Atlanta Hawks played the Golden State Warriors.

Schmitt revelled as a clearly flummoxed Smith struggled to discern what Schmitt was talking about.

"I don't think you know that we have this stuff," Schmitt said. "So I'll give you a second to process it so you don't perjure yourself."

After a few moments, Smith did recall having attended a basketball game — but not in Atlanta. It wasn't the Hawks his colleagues were discussing in a series of texts, Smith explained, but the Hawkeyes, whose star Caitlin Clark was playing in Maryland that day.

"It was because Caitlin Clark was coming to Maryland to play, and so we went to the game," Smith said.

Immediately after the exchange, Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) fact-checked Schmitt in real-time, confirming the date of the Iowa-Maryland game and suggested that her colleagues' reliance on "false information based on confusion about the name of a team" warranted an apology.

"You don't call someone a dirtbag when you haven't done your own research and you don't have your facts straight," Klobuchar said after the hearing. "And it just shows how completely out of control this whole thing was."

Schmitt did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his allegations.

Kelsey Brugger contributed to this report.

articles.body:
A Staten Island Judge on Tuesday ruled against New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s (D) pied-à-terre tax on second homes, arguing the city mishandled the tax’s rollout.

Judge Wayne Ozzi, a Democrat on the state’s Supreme Court, wrote in his ruling that Mamdani’s Department of Finance (DOF) violated the plaintiffs’s — a group of NYC homeowners — due process rights through its process of determining who would pay the tax on second homes worth more than $5 million.

“No crime is involved here, homeowners are being substantially harmed and penalized needlessly by DOF’s method of implementing the tax law,” Ozzi wrote.

He continued that the mailed notices the DOF sent to homeowners “irresponsibly and unnecessarily caused homeowners to expend time and money” and further “lacked any real guidance as to the proof required.”

Ozzi ordered the city to replace its roll that includes all homes that are subject to the tax with a limited roll “reflecting those properties actually subject to the surcharge.”

He also ordered that all previously mailed notices are canceled and new notices will be mailed “only after an individualized initial determination” can be made.

Ozzi issued a temporary restraining order in August to halt the tax’s rollout, but the city appealed, which halted the order from taking effect. This lawsuit does not challenge the legality of the tax but marks another setback for the rollout of the historic tax signed into law earlier this year.

“The way the Mamdani administration rolled this out is not only a total screwup, totally botched, a debacle,” Randy Mastro, the former first deputy mayor of NYC under former Mayor Eric Adams and the lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview with a Spectrum News local affiliate when the lawsuit was filed.

A spokesperson for Mamdani, Matt Rauschenbach, told The Hill the ruling was “wrong.”

“We will invoke a stay of the injunction. With a stay, we will continue implementing the surcharge fairly, efficiently and in full compliance with the law, as we have since day one,” he said.

Rauschenbach added that “the ultra-wealthy are fighting in court to avoid paying their fair share. They have filed lawsuit after lawsuit to protect their privilege, and we will not back down.”

A source from Mamdani’s administration said that the stay — which would pause the enforcement of Ozzi’s ruling — will be invoked Tuesday evening.

The tax was proposed by Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) in April, which they said at the time would help narrow the city’s budget deficit. It would be an annual surcharge on one- to three-family homes, condominiums and co-ops owned by people who have a separate primary residence.

Mamdani said in July that the tax was to provide the city with needed “long-term solutions” to its fiscal challenges.

In addition to his second-home tax, Mamdani has also faced legal pushback on his rent freeze plan, which landlords have characterized as overly punitive, his state-sponsored grocery store plan, which has sparked challenges from the National Supermarket Association and what they see as unfair competition and challenges to specialized high school admissions that some parents believe unfairly discriminates against Asian-American enrollees. articles.title: Unearthed audit exposes vulnerable Dem's handling of COVID relief funds: 'Gross oversight'
articles.summary: A federal audit found Rep. Jared Moskowitz's Florida Division of Emergency Management failed to monitor $1.23 billion in COVID-19 relief funding.
articles.body: During his time as director for the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM), Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., allowed over $1 billion in COVID-19 relief funding to go out the door without required monitoring, records reveal. The 2022 State of Florida Compliance and Internal Controls over Financial Reporting and Federal Awards flagged the weakness in its annual audit, stating, "FDEM did not monitor the activities of any subrecipients." While Fox News Digital is not aware of fraud that may have been committed with those funds, the resurfaced audit casts an unflattering light on Moskowitz as he pursues re-election in one of the country’s most competitive districts. It also raises questions about oversight efforts for state-level allocations for government funds, an issue Republicans have signaled merits more attention. COVID CASH MEANT TO GET KIDS BACK ON TRACK TOOK SURPRISING DETOUR IN BLUE-STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT Moskowitz’s FDEM approved $210,562,500 in funding to 39 local government recipients in the 2020-2021 fiscal year from the Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF), according to the audit. The next year, it distributed $1,026,225,200 to 55 locations. Taken together, the grants add up to $1.23 billion. "Contrary to Federal regulations, the FDEM did not monitor the activities of CRF subrecipients," the audit states. "Such monitoring is to include, for example, reviewing subrecipient audit reports and determining whether management decisions are required for any audit findings related to the federal award." According to the report, an acceptable level of oversight would normally include inquiries of the recipients as well as checks like onsite evaluations. "Monitoring of the subrecipient must include reviewing financial and performance reports, following up and ensuring that the subrecipient takes timely and appropriate action on all deficiencies pertaining to the federal award detected through audits, on-site reviews and other means," the audit states. MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER Notably, Moskowitz wasn’t head of FDEM for the entire 2020-2021 fiscal year. He resigned from the post at the end of April, two months before the end of the fiscal year in June, making him the head of the FDEM for the vast majority of the 2020-2021 audit cycle but not the complete window. Even so, his congressional opponent, Republican candidate Scott Singer, believes the responsibility lies squarely on Moskowitz’s shoulders. "When Jared Moskowitz ran a state agency, federal regulators and state auditors found that there was a gross lack of oversight of billions of dollars of taxpayer funds, a lack of reporting, a lack of review of where the funds were going," Singer said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And that's unacceptable, especially with public tax dollars. But it's not surprising." Singer argued the audit echoed earlier questions about Moskowitz's work involving disaster recovery funds. He pointed to an incident in 2017, when Moskowitz, as an attorney for AshBritt, a disaster-cleanup company, had renegotiated compensation from the City of Parkland after Hurricane Irma. Disclosure reports showed that he was being paid over $400,000 by the company while also serving as a state legislator. "When Jared was a state representative, he went to his own city and demanded that they pay more for hurricane cleanup that went to a disaster recovery company that paid him millions," Singer said. "We can't afford people who are continuing to do the same thing. A gross oversight of funds and self-dealing." When asked about Singer's criticisms, Moskowitz's campaign fired back, stating that the congressman was proud of the work that he did, noting that he had been reappointed to the role by a Republican governor. "As Director of FDEM, I worked directly for Governor DeSantis and his administration. Florida had one of the best COVID responses in the country," Moskowitz told Fox News Digital. TRUMP ANTI-FRAUD DIVISION'S FUTURE RESTS WITH SENATE DEMS AFTER BIPARTISAN HOUSE WIN "I left almost a year before this report was issued as I had to leave the agency to be with my dad, who was battling cancer. Governor DeSantis appointed me again to the Broward County commission. To my knowledge, Florida COVID spending has passed the FEMA audit for reimbursements," he added. Moskowitz also pointed out that he had received praise from even Republicans for his disaster-related work, including from Singer himself. Moskowitz shared communications between them in which Singer said the state was "in a much better place because of what you've done." Singer also highlighted a second communication from Singer to Moskowitz stating, "seriously, thank you for all of the amazing work you've done and all the help you're providing to our stay [sic]." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having cleared their parties’ respective primaries, Moskowitz and Singer will face off in the Florida general election Nov. 3.

articles.title: Jack Smith defends investigations into Trump during tense US Senate hearing
articles.summary: Former US special counsel rejects claims that his probes improperly targeted Republicans and conservative groups.
articles.body:
Former Special Counsel Jack Smith has defended his investigations of President Donald Trump in a United States Senate hearing, though Republican lawmakers accused him of abusing his authority.

On Tuesday, Smith told the Senate Judiciary Committee that his investigations followed Justice Department policy and were based on evidence.

He rejected accusations that political considerations influenced his decision to bring criminal charges against Trump, the first US president ever to be indicted.

“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation,” Smith said.

A former war crimes prosecutor at The Hague, Smith was appointed special counsel in 2022 to independently investigate allegations about Trump’s behaviour after the end of his first term as president.

In 2023, Smith ultimately brought two criminal indictments against Trump: one for his alleged attempts to subvert the 2020 presidential election and a second for his handling of classified documents while out of office.

Separately, two further criminal indictments were brought against Trump. One, in New York, accused Trump of falsifying business records to conceal unflattering information during his 2016 presidential campaign.

A second, in Georgia, also concerned allegations that Trump and his allies sought to overturn the 2020 election results.

Only one case – the New York indictment – was brought to trial, resulting in felony convictions. The rest were dropped after Trump was re-elected in 2024.

Smith himself resigned shortly before Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025. The Justice Department has a policy of not prosecuting sitting presidents.

Trump has denied all the charges against him and has accused Smith and former President Joe Biden of orchestrating a political “witch-hunt” against him.

Republicans focused much of Tuesday’s hearing on Smith’s investigative methods, including subpoenas that obtained phone records associated with members of Congress and financial information from Republican donors and organisations.

Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley accused Smith’s team of using its investigations to “map out and target the entire Republican Party”.

Smith, however, maintained that his office had a duty to pursue evidence relevant to the investigation.

He also defended obtaining phone records from lawmakers. He said the records helped corroborate evidence that Trump and his allies contacted members of Congress as they sought to delay certification of the 2020 election results.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, whose records were among those sought, pressed Smith about why lawmakers were not notified of the subpoenas. Smith said prosecutors feared Trump and his associates could destroy evidence or interfere with the investigation if the subpoenas were disclosed.

“Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Cruz asked.

Smith added that his office consulted the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section before obtaining the records.

The information Smith sought reveals the time and duration of the telephone calls but not their content. Critics have pointed out that there was no law against seeking such records during the course of Smith’s investigation.

During his testimony, Smith not only defended his investigative decisions but also accused the Trump administration of retaliating against the prosecutors and agents who worked on the two cases.

He argued that members of his former team had been fired for “doing their jobs”. Those firings have prompted legal challenges.

In March, three former agents with the FBI who investigated Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election filed a class-action lawsuit alleging they were illegally terminated as part of a “retribution campaign”. The lawsuit seeks their reinstatement.

Smith, who said Trump has threatened him with jail, framed the scrutiny of his work as part of a broader challenge to the independence of the Justice Department.

“As I appear before you today, it is my belief that the rule of law faces challenges unlike any we have experienced in our lifetime,” Smith said. “I will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”

articles.title: Trump says he plans to campaign for 32 days before midterm elections
articles.summary: US president brushes aside concerns about his popularity as voters express frustration over cost of living, war on Iran.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has announced that he will spend 32 days travelling and campaigning for the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.

The upcoming race is widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term in office, and it could decide whether his political agenda faces legislative hurdles for the next two years.

Trump has even speculated that, if Democrats take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, he could face a third impeachment.

Still, on Tuesday, Trump expressed optimism as he spoke to reporters. He also denied that Republican candidates are seeking to distance themselves from his administration ahead of the vote.

“You love me, and I love them,” Trump said, as he outlined his plans for a multi-state tour to support Republican midterm contenders.

“Just so you understand, they all want me to go. I’m one person. They all want me to go campaign,” he added.

Trump described his travel itinerary as “literally a 32-day tour”, set to include visits to states such as Texas and Ohio, where toss-up races are under way.

But critics have speculated that Trump’s slipping popularity could spell trouble for the Republican Party, which hopes to hold onto its majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Recent polls suggest that Trump’s approval has fallen to new lows as voters express frustration over the rising cost of living , caused in part by Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran that has roiled global energy markets.

A Wall Street Journal poll released last week found that Trump’s approval rating sits at 37 percent.

That marks the lowest rate for a president in the lead-up to the midterms since the outlet began conducting the poll in 1990, when George HW Bush was in office.

Still, Trump has positioned himself as a central figure in the Republican Party’s bid to win the midterm races.

This month, the party held its first-ever midterm political convention in Texas, with Trump delivering a keynote address.

Trump’s allies have also pledged that the Republican leader would “campaign like it’s 2024 again”, a reference to his successful second bid for the presidency.

Supporters have speculated he could have success in mobilising so-called low-propensity voters, who are considered less likely to cast a ballot.

Some of his tactics have attracted outcry, however. The Department of Homeland Security, which has played a central role in Trump’s mass deportation push, has recently come under scrutiny for using $20m to create campaign-style advertisements lauding the Republican leader’s accomplishments.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have slammed those efforts as an inappropriate use of taxpayer funds that could violate anti-propaganda laws.

“We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars,” Democratic Senator Patty Murray wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a letter on Tuesday.
