articles.title: Eleições 2026: como votar em trânsito? | G1
articles.standfirst: Por essa modalidade, quem estiver fora da cidade onde vota em outubro poderá participar da eleição em outro ponto do país. O prazo para solicitar o voto em trânsito, porém, já terminou.
articles.summary: Por essa modalidade, quem estiver fora da cidade onde vota em outubro poderá participar da eleição em outro ponto do país. O prazo para solicitar o voto em trânsito, porém, já term
articles.body:
Eleitores que optarem pelo voto em trânsito nas Eleições 2026 poderão votar fora da cidade onde têm domicílio eleitoral. O prazo para solicitar a modalidade terminou em 20 de agosto.

A opção estará disponível nas capitais e em municípios com mais de 100 mil eleitores. Os locais de votação serão definidos pelos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs).

Veja abaixo como funciona o voto em trânsito.

O voto em trânsito permite que cidadãos que estão fora da cidade onde votam participem da eleição em outro local.

A modalidade existe nas eleições gerais, quando são escolhidos presidente, governadores, senadores e deputados federais, estaduais e distritais.

A pessoa que estiver em cidades diferentes nos dois turnos da eleição pode solicitar a habilitação para votar em trânsito em uma cidade distinta em cada turno.

Após as eleições, o título retornará à seção eleitoral de origem automaticamente, o que dispensa a necessidade de pedir a transferência de volta ao domicílio eleitoral original.

Em quais cargos o eleitor pode votar nesta situação?

Isso depende de onde o eleitor estará no dia da votação. Quem estiver no mesmo estado, mas em outra cidade, pode votar para presidente da República, governador, senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual ou distrital.

Já quem estiver fora do estado onde vota poderá escolher apenas o presidente da República.

Como funciona para quem mora no exterior?

Brasileiros que moram no exterior e estarão no país durante as eleições também podem usar o voto em trânsito.

Quem tem título registrado no exterior pode votar no Brasil em outubro, desde que solicite o voto em trânsito no mesmo prazo para quem mora no Brasil.

O que acontece se o eleitor não comparecer?

O eleitor que se inscreveu para o voto em trânsito e não pôde comparecer deve justificar a ausência, mesmo que esteja na cidade onde tem inscrição eleitoral no dia da eleição.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: qual a ordem de votação na urna? | G1
articles.standfirst: Eleitor fará seis escolhas no primeiro turno das eleições. O g1 preparou uma 'colinha' para os leitores preencherem com seus candidatos escolhidos.
articles.summary: Eleitor fará seis escolhas no primeiro turno das eleições. O g1 preparou uma 'colinha' para os leitores preencherem com seus candidatos escolhidos.
articles.body:
No próximo domingo, dia 4 de outubro, o eleitor brasileiro vai fazer seis escolhas nas urnas para as Eleições 2026.

No primeiro turno, o eleitor deverá seguir a seguinte ordem:

Primeiro, vota para deputado federal (quatro dígitos).

Em seguida, é a vez de votar para deputado estadual ou distrital, no caso do DF (cinco dígitos).

Na sequência, aparece a tela para votar na primeira vaga para senador (três dígitos).

Assim que a urna computar este voto, o eleitor vota novamente para senador (três dígitos).

Na sequência, escolhe o governador do seu estado (dois dígitos).

E, por fim, vota para presidente da República (dois dígitos).

A cada etapa, confira os dados que aparecem na tela, como a foto do candidato, o nome, o número e o partido, antes de apertar a tecla verde de “Confirma” e passar para o próximo cargo em disputa.

❗ATENÇÃO: ao votar nas duas vagas para o Senado, para que os dois votos sejam válidos, é necessário escolher nomes diferentes. Se o eleitor repetir e confirmar o mesmo candidato nas duas opções, o segundo voto será anulado.

Se houver apenas uma disputa pendente, o eleitor votará somente para aquele cargo no segundo turno.

No dia da eleição, é possível levar um cola eleitoral já com a ordem de votação na urna para ajudar o eleitor ao fazer suas escolhas. No entanto, esta cola deve ser de papel. articles.title: TSE julga nesta quarta posts sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida | G1
articles.standfirst: Análise ocorrerá no plenário virtual. Ministros vão analisar decisão de André Mendonça que removeu as publicações que associavam Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a uma suposta iniciativa para retirar de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil.
articles.summary: O plenário do TSE analisa a remoção de posts sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida e Flávio Bolsonaro após decisões divergentes dos ministros André Mendonça e Flávio Dino.
articles.body:
O plenário virtual do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) vai analisar nesta quarta-feira (30) a decisão do ministro André Mendonça que removeu as publicações que associavam o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a um suposto movimento de retirada de Nossa Senhora Aparecida do posto de padroeira do Brasil.

A análise está prevista para começar às 10h e vai até às 23h59 desta quarta.

Com a decisão, Fux restabeleceu, até a análise pelo plenário do STF , a determinação de Mendonça para retirar do ar as postagens, que incluíam a uma publicação do humorista Antonio Tabet.

A decisão de Dino, tomada no domingo (27), havia permitido o restabelecimento do post de Tabet e de outras publicações removidas pelo mesmo fundamento.

Dino argumentou que a postagem não citava nominalmente Flávio Bolsonaro e que a medida era necessária para proteger a liberdade de expressão.

Fux, que atendeu a um pedido da defesa do candidato, defendeu que o tema fosse examinado pelo colegiado diante dos impactos sobre a Justiça Eleitoral e sobre a disputa presidencial em curso.

O presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin, chegou a sinalizar que pautaria o assunto nesta quarta-feira (30), o que não chegou a ser confirmado.

Fachada do prédio do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) — Foto: Luiz Roberto/Secom/tse

Perto de completar um mês, a crise institucional vivida pelo STF provoca impactos no TSE, na reta final do primeiro turno.

A ala alinhada ao ministro André Mendonça chegou a procurar o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, na segunda para questionar ações de aliados do ministro Alexandre de Moraes que, na avaliação desses integrantes da Corte, tentam arrastar a Corte Eleitoral.

A tentativa desse grupo de ministros era acelerar o julgamento no plenário da decisão de Dino que derrubou a ordem de Mendonça, tomada no TSE, para que plataformas excluíssem postagens sobre a discussão em torno do título de padroeira de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

Em outra frente, os aliados de Moraes indicavam que uma discussão na véspera da eleição poderia expor ainda mais o tribunal e acirrar a erosão interna na cúpula do Judiciário.

"Eu tenho a convicção de que tentaram matar o meu pai porque viram que ele já era presidente do Brasil em 2018. Por isso, foram para tentar eliminá-lo. Foi aquela facada, lá em Juiz de Fora... Para você ver, mais uma vez. Eu acho que eu posso considerar uma espécie de facada essa fake news em mim", disse o candidato ao SantoFlow Podcast.

"Enquanto eu for presidente da República, ninguém vai avacalhar com Nossa Senhora Aparecida. Ninguém. As pessoas precisam aprender a respeitar todas as religiões, inclusive as religiões de matriz africana. É preciso. Ninguém é dono da verdade. A única igreja mentirosa é aquela da Lagoinha, daquele pastor chamado Valadão, que era sócio do Vorcaro", afirmou Lula.

A Igreja Batista da Lagoinha tem sede em Belo Horizonte, em Minas Gerais, e recebeu repasses por investigados ligados ao ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, segundo relatórios do Conselho de Controle de Atividades Financeiras (Coaf).

articles.title: Pais e maridos: candidatos recorrem a nomes de parentes na urna | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do g1 identificou 39 pessoas que incorporaram o nome de familiares ou de aliados políticos ao nome de urna.
articles.summary: O g1 identificou ao menos 39 pessoas que incorporaram o nome de familiares ou de aliados políticos e chegam às urnas como candidatos que pertencem a alguém.
articles.body:
Levantamento do g1 com base nas candidaturas registradas no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) nestas eleições 2026 revela que ao menos 39 candidatos incorporaram ao nome de urna uma menção a outra pessoa. Dezesseis deles fazem isso pela primeira vez, enquanto os demais já usaram essa estratégia de identificação em eleições passadas.

Segundo a cientista política Danusa Marques, professora do Instituto de Ciência Política da Universidade de Brasília (IPOL/UnB), o fenômeno mostra a tentativa de se associar a alguém já reconhecido socialmente. De acordo com os dados, esse alguém é, na maioria das vezes, um parente homem do candidato ou candidata.

Dos 39 candidatos, 32 mencionam familiares e 2 fazem alusão a aliados políticos. Em cinco casos, não foi possível confirmar a relação entre o candidato e a pessoa citada.

Entre os 32 casos de parentesco identificados, 14 candidatos fazem menção aos pais; 11 candidatas, aos maridos; 3, aos filhos; e 3, às mães. Em um caso, não foi possível determinar se o nome de urna faz referência ao pai ou à mãe.

Os cinco casos em que o vínculo não pôde ser confirmado têm características de possíveis patronímicos — nomes formados a partir da referência a um antepassado do candidato.

Homens são maioria dos referenciados por candidatos. — Foto: Kayan Albertin / Arte g1

Entre as 38 pessoas identificadas pelo g1 como referenciadas pelos candidatos, 20 ocupam ou já ocuparam cargos políticos. Outros quatro nomes usados por candidatos são de comerciantes, dois são de crianças com necessidades de cuidados especiais, dois são patriarcas de famílias tradicionais, um é de uma liderança local e outro é de um jogador de futebol. Em oito casos, não foi possível confirmar a atividade ou trajetória da pessoa mencionada.

Para analisar o fenômeno, Marques diferencia famílias políticas de dinastias políticas. A família política é quando alguém tem um parente que ocupa cargo público, seja eletivo ou de confiança. Já a dinastia política é caracterizada por famílias que têm várias gerações ocupando posições de poder, principalmente em cargos eletivos.

O que há em comum em todos os candidatos identificados no levantamento, observa Marques, é a tentativa de se associar a alguém já reconhecido. “O objetivo é se vincular a quem tem posição relevante naquele contexto, seja no estado, na cidade ou em uma comunidade”, disse a especialista.

Segundo Marques, a escolha de carregar outra pessoa no nome de urna deixa claro o acesso que esses candidatos têm a uma rede de contatos e de aprendizado político.

"Existe um capital político, e não necessariamente é o sobrenome, ou só a referência explícita a alguém. Essas pessoas aprenderam as regras da política, aprenderam como se portar, o que fazer e quais são as estratégias possíveis", disse a especialista.

Ela ressalta ainda que o uso do nome na urna é apenas um recorte do universo das famílias políticas. “Além desses candidatos, existem muitos outros que usam apenas o sobrenome que já possuem, por fazerem parte de uma família tradicional na política”, disse a especialista.

Imagem urna eletrônica — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Sergipe é o estado em que mais candidatos incorporaram nomes de outras pessoas no registro de candidatura, segundo o levantamento do g1 . São nove. A Bahia aparece em segundo lugar como estado onde o fenômeno mais acontece, com seis candidatos identificados.

Em Pernambuco, no Rio de Janeiro e em Minas Gerais, o g1 encontrou quatro candidatos em cada estado. Já a Paraíba, o Ceará e Rondônia têm dois candidatos cada, enquanto o Distrito Federal e os estados de Tocantins, Alagoas, Maranhão, São Paulo e Goiás têm um candidato cada.

34 candidatos fazem referência a homens; só 3 referenciam mulheres

As diferenças de gênero aparecem nos nomes escolhidos para a urna por esse grupo de candidatos. Trinta e quatro deles fazem referência a homens e apenas três, a mulheres, mais especificamente às mães. Em dois casos, não foi possível determinar o gênero da pessoa mencionada.

Para Marques, isso é reflexo da predominância masculina nos espaços de poder. “As mulheres nunca chegaram a mais de 20% de cadeiras na Câmara e no Senado. Então, se alguém quer se apoiar num nome com proeminência política, muito provavelmente vai ser um homem”, disse a pesquisadora.

O Brasil aparece em 133º lugar no mundo no ranking de participação de mulheres nos parlamentos nacionais, elaborado pela Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU). Na América Latina, está entre os países com pior representação feminina no Legislativo.

"É importante não naturalizar o fato de a maior parte dos espaços de poder serem ocupados por homens no Brasil. Isso não é algo comum, não é um padrão mundial, é algo do Brasil e mostra o nosso atraso em termos de democratização", disse a pesquisadora.

O levantamento expõe outro aspecto da política para as mulheres. Ao menos 11 candidatas usam o nome do marido na urna, e 10 desses homens ocupam ou já ocuparam cargos políticos; em um caso, não foi possível confirmar a trajetória da pessoa mencionada.

Das 11 mulheres, 10 recorreram às preposições “de” ou “do”, construções que remetem à ideia de posse. Segundo Marques, a referência aos maridos é um reforço do padrão patriarcal na política.

Nem sempre o nome que o candidato incorpora vem de uma geração anterior ou do marido. Em dois casos, as mães escolheram se identificar na urna pelos nomes dos próprios filhos. Em outro, foi um pai que fez o mesmo.

Marques avalia que candidatas constroem suas trajetórias políticas a partir da ideia do cuidado, especificamente como mães. "É uma militância. É diferente de se apoiar em outras pessoas que já têm carreiras políticas”, disse a pesquisadora.

Já o pai, que usa o nome do filho jogador de futebol, segue outra lógica. “É alguém que está tentando apelar para a popularidade de uma pessoa famosa”, avalia Marques.

articles.title: Veja as propostas dos candidatos a presidente para segurança, combate à corrupção, STF, salário mínimo e outros temas | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamentos do g1 reuniram as propostas dos candidatos à Presidência para áreas como salário mínimo, aposentadorias, impostos e segurança pública; confira os principais pontos dos planos de governo.
articles.summary: Levantamentos do g1 reuniram as propostas dos candidatos à Presidência para áreas como salário mínimo, aposentadorias, impostos e segurança pública; confira os principais pontos dos planos de governo.
articles.body:
Uma série de reportagens publicadas pelo g1 ao longo da campanha eleitoral mostrou quais são as propostas dos candidatos à Presidência da República para temas que estão entre as principais preocupações dos brasileiros.

Para fazer as reportagens, a equipe de jornalistas analisou os planos de governo que cada candidato registrou no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Pesquisa Quaest divulgada na última segunda-feira (28) mostra que violência (29%), corrupção (21%) e economia (19%) são as preocupações mais citadas pelos eleitores.

As propostas dos presidenciáveis focam na ampliação dos mecanismos de rastreamento do orçamento, na modernização da fiscalização de contratos estatais e no fortalecimento de órgãos de controle e punições. As medidas vão desde inteligência artificial para o combate de crimes contra o patrimônio público até confisco de bens dos condenados por corrupção.

Sessão plenária extraordinária do STF sobre o caso Moraes — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

Após novos desdobramentos no caso Master, a crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) virou tema da campanha presidencial. Propostas para uma reforma no Judiciário variam nos planos de governo, desde ajustes na dinâmica de decisões monocráticas e tempo de mandato para magistrados até reformulações nas regras de indicação e na estrutura do Judiciário.

Os feminicídios bateram recorde no Brasil em 2025, com uma média de quatro mulheres mortas por dia por razões de gênero. Enquanto as mulheres são maioria do eleitorado brasileiro, o debate sobre a escalada da violência contra a mulher ganhou espaço nas propostas dos candidatos. Os programas eleitorais englobam a expansão das redes de acolhimento especializado, o fortalecimento de tecnologias de monitoramento e o endurecimento de penas e regras de prisão para agressores.

Supersalários e penduricalhos no setor público

Os chamados “supersalários” e “penduricalhos” estão no centro de propostas em discussão nos Três Poderes. As verbas que ultrapassam o limite do funcionalismo público, só em 2025, custaram mais de R$ 10 bilhões aos cofres públicos. As diretrizes dos candidatos à Presidência abordam a limitação de verbas indenizatórias e benefícios extras, buscando aplicar com rigor o limite salarial estabelecido pela Constituição nos Três Poderes.

O reajuste das aposentadorias e dos benefícios previdenciários está vinculado ao salário mínimo, e esse é um dos pontos centrais em discussão nos planos de governo dos candidatos à Presidência. As propostas dos presidenciáveis dividem-se entre a manutenção ou alteração das regras de valorização do salário mínimo, reajustes nos benefícios sociais e medidas para assegurar a sustentabilidade da Previdência.

Edifício-sede do BC em Brasília, onde a decisão sobre a taxa de juros é tomada — Foto: Foto: Adobe stock - Banco Central.

A taxa básica de juros, a Selic, afeta diretamente o acesso ao crédito, os investimentos produtivos e o grau de endividamento das famílias brasileiras. Os planos dos presidenciáveis propõe diferentes estratégias para a redução do custo do dinheiro, o controle da inflação, o equilíbrio da dívida pública e programas voltados à renegociação de débitos dos consumidores.

O posicionamento diplomático do Brasil define a inserção comercial do país no mercado global, suas alianças estratégicas e a atração de capital estrangeiro. As propostas dos candidatos incluem a aproximação de países da Ásia e da África, dos Estados Unidos, fortalecimento do Mercosul e saída do Brics. Com diferentes abordagens, os planos de governo detalham rumos para o fortalecimento das exportações, a soberania do Brasil perante o mundo e a celebração de acordos internacionais.

O controle das divisas territoriais do país é peça estratégica para coibir a entrada de armas e drogas que abastecem as redes de crime organizado nas cidades. Diante da escalada no combate do tráfico de drogas no contexto da América do Sul, as propostas dos presidenciáveis focam no fortalecimento da integração entre forças de segurança, na expansão de acordos de cooperação com países vizinhos e em investimentos em tecnologias de vigilância territorial.

Paraíba tem maior crescimento populacional do Nordeste entre 2025 e 2026 — Foto: Rizemberg Felipe/Jornal da Paraíba

A Região Nordeste é estratégica no cenário eleitoral e socioeconômico do país, demandando políticas públicas focadas na redução das desigualdades regionais e no crescimento sustentável. As diretrizes apresentadas pelos presidenciáveis buscam impulsionar a economia local com investimentos em infraestrutura e segurança hídrica, além de explorar o potencial da região para a geração de energias renováveis e a atração de novos polos tecnológicos.

A sensação de insegurança e a atuação de facções criminosas colocam a segurança pública no topo das prioridades apontadas pelo eleitorado em todo o país. As ações propostas pelos candidatos cobrem o combate a grupos armados, a reestruturação e modernização das corporações policiais, a reformulação do sistema penitenciário e ações de inteligência.

O que há de comum entre os planos de governo

Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos e Romeu Zema — Foto: Globo

Adversários na eleição presidencial de 2026, os seis candidatos mais bem colocados nas pesquisas de intenção de voto apresentam propostas convergentes para temas detalhados em seus planos de governo.

Tanto o presidente Lula (PT) quanto os adversários da oposição, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Renan Santos (Missão), Augusto Cury (Avante) e Romeu Zema (Novo), defendem propostas iguais ou similares em cinco assuntos nos planos de governo enviados à Justiça Eleitoral.

articles.title: O que são bancadas e frentes parlamentares? | G1
articles.standfirst: Entenda como deputados e senadores se organizam no Congresso. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Entenda como deputados e senadores se organizam no Congresso. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:
Depois de eleitos, deputados e senadores também se organizam em grupos dentro do Congresso para atuar em torno de interesses e pautas em comum.

O termo bancada pode ter diferentes significados. Formalmente, pode designar os parlamentares de um mesmo partido ou bloco. Mas também é usado, de maneira informal, para reunir congressistas do mesmo estado ou ligados a uma determinada pauta — como as chamadas bancadas do agro, evangélica, da segurança, feminina e negra.

Já as frentes parlamentares são associações suprapartidárias formadas por deputados e senadores em torno de determinado tema. Para serem registradas oficialmente na Câmara, precisam do apoio de pelo menos um terço dos integrantes do Congresso — atualmente, 198 parlamentares. A regra existe desde 2005.

Entre as frentes de maior alcance estão a Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária (FPA), conhecida como bancada do agro; a Frente Parlamentar da Segurança Pública; a Frente Parlamentar Evangélica; e a Frente Parlamentar do Empreendedorismo. Elas reúnem parlamentares de diferentes partidos que atuam em torno de pautas e interesses comuns.

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 explica os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

articles.title: Falta de água em Guaratinguetá: furto na Saeg afeta 6 bairros | G1
articles.standfirst: Companhia informou que equipes trabalham para recuperar o sistema após ocorrência durante a madrugada desta quarta-feira (30).
articles.summary: Falta de água em Guaratinguetá atinge seis bairros após furto em unidade da Saeg nesta quarta (30); equipes trabalham para normalizar o sistema.
articles.body:
Torneira sem água. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

Um furto em uma unidade da Companhia de Serviço de Água, Esgoto e Resíduos de Guaratinguetá (Saeg) pode afetar o abastecimento de água em seis bairros da cidade nesta quarta-feira (30).

Segundo a Saeg, a unidade foi alvo de furto durante a madrugada. A ocorrência comprometeu o funcionamento do sistema de abastecimento e, por isso, moradores das regiões afetadas podem registrar falta de água ou baixa pressão nas torneiras.

Os bairros que podem ter o abastecimento afetado são Santa Luzia, Los Angeles, Parque das Garças, Itália, Espanha e Municipal.

A companhia informou que equipes técnicas foram mobilizadas para realizar os serviços necessários à recuperação do sistema. O trabalho tem como objetivo restabelecer o abastecimento de forma gradual e no menor prazo possível.

A Saeg não informou quais equipamentos ou materiais foram furtados da unidade. Também não foram divulgadas informações sobre suspeitos ou sobre o registro da ocorrência policial.

A orientação é que os moradores das áreas afetadas acompanhem a situação enquanto os trabalhos são realizados e façam uso consciente da água que estiver disponível durante o período de instabilidade no abastecimento.

Em caso de dúvidas ou necessidade de atendimento, os moradores podem entrar em contato com a Saeg pelo telefone 156 ou pelo aplicativo 156 Saeg.

articles.title: ‘F--- her’: Jasmine Crockett torched by ex-Dem colleague over who she left off endorsement list
articles.summary: Former Rep. Susan Wild unleashed a profane tirade against Jasmine Crockett after the Texas Democrat's FIRE PAC endorsement list omitted James Talarico.
articles.body: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, drew backlash from a former colleague for leaving James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas, off her list of endorsements Monday. Talarico, who beat Crockett in the party’s Senate primary earlier this year, was not among 14 candidates supported by Crockett’s Feuling Individual Rights Everywhere (FIRE) PAC. To former Rep. Susan Wild, D-Pa., who served three terms in Congress, the list is clear evidence Crockett is putting personal reservations over the party’s success in the Lone Star State. "F--- her. That’s all I can say. And that statement has nothing to do with blind loyalty to Dems," Wild said in a post to X. "It has everything to do with her being a narcissistic drama queen who has used her platform (such as it is) only to advance herself. Karma will suck." Wild’s post is just the most recent controversy surrounding Crockett, a progressive who has called on her party to inch further left through fiery rhetoric that’s garnered national attention during her time in Congress. LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP In the past, Crockett has drawn scrutiny for incendiary comments, like calling Gov. Greg Abbott, who is permanently in a wheelchair, "Governor Hot Wheels," describing Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., as having a "beach-blond, bad-built, butch body," and describing MAGA Latino voters as having a "slave mentality." Most recently, Crockett received public backlash for entering Chris Brown into the congressional record, honoring his musical legacy in the Black community despite a history of violence against women. JASMINE CROCKETT TORCHED FOR HONORING SINGER WITH NOTORIOUS HISTORY OF VIOLENCE: 'COMPLETELY VILE' Crockett posted her own reply to Wild and others, noting that she had personally extended congratulations to Talarico after he beat her earlier this year in the March primary. "Y’all are corny! Keep receipts. I’ll be happy when people either give a damn about FACTS or news media goes back to the news instead of deciding to ride the tabloid lane. NOW FOR THE 1000th time maybe write an article about KEN F*in PAXTON. Y’all sound like corny groupies," Crockett wrote. Crockett, who lost to Talarico by a margin of 52.4% to 46.2%, did endorse Talarico the day after the election after results were finalized. "This morning I called James and congratulated him on becoming the Senate nominee. Texas is primed to turn blue, and we must remain united because this is bigger than any one person. This is about the future of all 30 million Texans and getting America back on track. With the primary behind us, Democrats must rally around our nominees and win," Crockett wrote. "I’m committed to doing my part and will continue working to elect Democrats up and down the ballot." SHOCK POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD Crockett’s FIRE PAC has raised only $144,960 and mostly focuses on smaller races. All 14 candidates listed on the post highlighted by Wild are state or local candidates. Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa was also not on the list. articles.title: Boeing lands $20B-plus Navy deal for sixth-generation fighter to deliver ‘absolute air superiority’
articles.summary: Boeing's $20 billion F/A-XX contract marks the Navy's first sixth-generation fighter, designed to replace F/A-18 Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers.
articles.body: The U.S. Navy has tapped Boeing to build a new fighter jet that officials say will help American pilots dominate the skies, defeat enemies and come home safely. The Department of War announced Tuesday that Boeing secured a contract worth more than $20 billion for full-scale development of the F/A-XX, a sixth-generation strike fighter intended to expand the reach of Navy aircraft carriers and eventually replace some of the service’s longtime combat aircraft. The deal gives Boeing its second sixth-generation fighter program following its selection for the Air Force’s F-47 in 2025, the company said. "Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly. We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs," Steve Parker, president and CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a statement. EUROPE'S $116B FIGHTER JET 'FAILURE' RAISES FRESH DOUBTS ABOUT ABILITY TO DEFEND ITSELF WITHOUT US The Navy contract includes multiple test aircraft for ground testing, airworthiness evaluations and systems and weapons integration, according to the Department of War. STARTUPS BRING INNOVATION TO DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE "The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength. F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter," Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment, said in the announcement. Duffey called the aircraft a "crucial, non-negotiable investment" in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities. PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION "We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities rapidly, ensuring our warfighters possess the lethal and highly networked systems required to deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority," he said. The F/A-XX falls under the Next Generation Air Dominance program. The department said the carrier-based fighter will extend the Navy’s operational reach and work alongside both manned and unmanned aircraft, including Collaborative Combat Aircraft. BATTLEFIELD ROBOTS OPEN NEW FRONT IN INNOVATION WAR WITH MAJOR US ADVERSARY Officials said the fighter will also increase the capability of the unmanned aircraft it teams with. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao hailed the contract as the beginning of "a new era" for the service. TRUMP TAPS ‘TRUE WARRIOR’ HUNG CAO AS NAVY SECRETARY AFTER 4 MONTHS AS ACTING LEADER "The Sixth-Generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe," Cao said. "We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies." AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX Boeing said the aircraft will bring advances in mission systems and operational reach and capacity, though technical and program details remain classified under U.S. national security and export laws. "It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform," Parker said, adding that the company’s team is "ready to execute this critical program." INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE The company said construction continues on a secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis as it prepares to build multiple aircraft with next-generation capabilities. "Investment in facilities is just one part of the story; we’re also investing in technology and people so that we can deliver for our customers," Parker said. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe celebrated the announcement, pointing to the state’s role in building America’s next generation of military aircraft. "St. Louis is Fighterland, USA!" Kehoe wrote on X. "Proud of this incredible win that further cements Missouri as a critical leader in the future of America’s air dominance, innovation, and national defense." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Beginning in the 2030s, the F/A-XX is expected to augment and eventually replace legacy F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers, according to the Department of War. It will also operate alongside the F-35C.

articles.title: Venezuelan national shot by ICE officer in Austin charged with assaulting federal officer
articles.summary: The Justice Department charged Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez with assaulting a federal officer after an Austin vehicle pursuit ended in an ICE shooting.
articles.body: A Venezuelan national who was shot by an ICE officer following a vehicle pursuit in Austin earlier this month has been charged with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer, the Justice Department announced Tuesday. Federal prosecutors allege that Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, refused ICE officers' commands to exit his vehicle during a targeted traffic stop before speeding away and striking one officer in the torso with his driver's side-view mirror. Garces-Perez faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted, according to DOJ. According to the complaint, officers first spotted Garces-Perez's vehicle outside a restaurant, ran its license plate and confirmed that an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal against him before initiating the stop. AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION The accounts differ over whether the vehicles made contact as officers stopped Garces-Perez. The officer told investigators there was no contact between the vehicles, while Garces-Perez claimed the ICE SUV's maneuver caused a collision before the officers approached him. During the encounter, Garces-Perez provided officers with his driver's license, according to the complaint. The officers described the initial encounter as "pleasant and not aggressive," according to the complaint. After officers instructed Garces-Perez to place the vehicle in park and step out, body camera footage shows him abruptly closing his window and driving away, according to the complaint. EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET Garces-Perez later told federal investigators that he disregarded the officers' command to exit the vehicle and drove away, according to the complaint. The complaint states that he was read his Miranda rights in Spanish, said he understood them and agreed to speak with investigators without an attorney present. As he drove away, Garces-Perez's driver's side-view mirror struck one of the officers in the torso, according to the complaint. According to the complaint, ICE officers pursued Garces-Perez through commercial and residential areas with emergency lights and sirens activated. The officer wearing a body camera lost sight of both Garces-Perez and the second ICE officer while requesting assistance from a DPS dispatcher and then turned off his camera, according to the complaint. The second officer, who later fired his weapon, was not equipped with a body camera. DEM REACTIONS WITHIN MOMENTS OF AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARK VIRAL OUTRAGE LOCALLY, ONLINE: 'DISQUALIFYING' The second officer later called his partner and reported that Garces-Perez had attempted to strike him with his vehicle, prompting the officer to fire his service weapon, according to the complaint. Garces-Perez was struck by a bullet in his upper back, according to the complaint. He told investigators that the officer's SUV rammed his vehicle to force it into a spinout and that, after he was shot, the officer opened his driver's door, removed the keys from the ignition and told him to remain inside while an ambulance was en route. Garces-Perez's immigration case has also been the subject of competing claims. Fox News previously reported that his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said the order was issued after a hearing notice was sent to an old address despite Garces-Perez having updated his address with the court. TRUMP REVIVES SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION SHOWDOWN AFTER HOCHUL PARDON TORPEDOED FIRST CASE ICE has disputed claims surrounding his immigration status, saying his work authorization expired in 2025 and that a work permit does not itself confer lawful immigration status. His attorney has said Garces-Perez remains seriously ill and has a bullet lodged in his body while being held at an ICE detention facility. Lincoln-Goldfinch, responding to the criminal complaint in a social media post, called for DHS to release the body camera footage. "The criminal complaint also provides another critical piece of information: one of the officers involved in the incident had a body camera that was turned off at some point during the pursuit. We have not seen that footage. DHS must release the body camera footage immediately and provide full transparency to the American public," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote. "He is now facing proceedings in both a federal criminal case and his federal immigration habeas case. We are working through what these developments mean, and we will share additional information as we are able." DOJ said Garces-Perez made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A detention hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2.

articles.title: Mark Carney's stand against Trump leads to Nobel Peace Prize and Time Person of the Year buzz
articles.summary: Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump.  If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right...
articles.body:
TORONTO (AP) — Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine's Person of the Year.

Carney briefly became the favorite Monday for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Kalshi , a U.S.-based prediction market, when traders on the exchange put his chances at 14%. His odds later fell, illustrating the highly speculative nature of the wagering.

There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee's secret shortlist for the prize that will be announced Oct. 9 in Oslo, Norway.

But the buzz about the Canadian leader possibly winning the esteemed peace prize reflects the message that has raised his profile: Middle powers should band together to defend sovereignty as great powers increasingly use economic and military leverage.

Whether that position resonates with the Nobel Committee is impossible to know. One thing is certain, though: the Nobel and Time's annual award happen to be two honors Trump covets .

Carney and Trump are locked in an escalating trade war , with 50% U.S. tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods and Canadian retaliation. Trump also has told Canadian leaders to "fall in line" or face consequences "far WORSE" than existing tariffs.

Trump, who has twice been Time's Person of the Year, has repeatedly complained about not receiving the Nobel, saying in July that he "should have won that award more than anybody."

"President Trump would be furious, of course," said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. "If this ever happens, I would love to be a fly on the wall of the Oval Office to see the president's face when he learns about it."

Trump already possesses a Nobel medal, just not one awarded to him.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel laureate, presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Trump accepted it, while the Nobel Committee stressed the prize itself remains hers.

"Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," said Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are."

Time already named Carney one of its 100 most influential people of 2026 and specifically noted his popularity increased as he stood up to Trump.

On Tuesday, Carney was the second choice on major prediction markets for Time's Person of the Year, behind New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The winner will be announced Dec. 10.

Time has described Trump's cumulative impact as helping create a "new global order" increasingly shaped "not by systems or institutions, but by the will of a single man." Carney's answer has been to urge middle powers to band together rather than bend one by one.

New York University professor Scott Galloway said Carney has it in the bag and called him "the leader that Europe's been looking for for the last 20 years."

"I believe, hands down, Time's Person of the Year has already been decided and it's going to be Mark Carney," Galloway said.

On Galloway's podcast, journalist Fareed Zakaria said Carney is winning admiration abroad and has given countries facing a less predictable United States "a kind of language and a path" to build new alliances rather than simply bend to Washington.

Carney moving to front of a new global order

Carney's standing abroad took off in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where he declared the old international order was not coming back and urged middle powers to work together rather than wait for its restoration. His speech came as European leaders were confronting Trump's push to acquire Greenland and tariff threats.

"We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition," Carney said in his speech, which received a standing ovation.

Carney has since tried to put the argument for a new global order into practice, pushing Canada closer to Europe and seeking new partners in Asia as Trump's tariffs fractured the old Canada-U.S. relationship.

European lawmakers gave Carney another standing ovation this month as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the European Union's first associate member .

"Carney's international profile has been driven by his standing up to Trump, unlike the Europeans and Asians who rushed to make deals with him," Wiseman said. "Trump's pressure on Canada has helped elevate Carney in the eyes of the world."

articles.title: Hegseth to cut number of US general and admiral positions by 20%
articles.summary: Pentagon official says the plan will be announced in the defence secretary’s ‘State of the Force’ address in Virginia.
articles.body:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will cut the number of positions reserved for generals and admirals by 20 percent, a Pentagon official has told Al Jazeera, in a change that will affect leadership across the Army, Navy and Air Force.

Hegseth is expected to announce the decision on Wednesday during a visit to the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, where he will deliver his “State of the Force” address in front of junior officers and enlisted officials, the official said.

The Associated Press news agency, citing Pentagon officials, reported that Hegseth will direct all the military services to double the 10 percent reduction that he ordered last year to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. This would make it a 20 percent total decrease and is to be completed by January 1, 2027.

Fox News reported the new reductions could include any one-star general or above or officer of equivalent Navy rank.

The Washing Post reported that the cuts could affect the careers of “hundreds of current and rising military leaders following scores of firings and denied promotions”.

US President Donald Trump or Hegseth have fired, or pushed into retirement, more than two dozen military leaders since taking office in January 2025, including the Army’s top uniformed officer, General Randy George , in April.

The administration also fired the only two women serving as four-star officers, along with several other senior female officers. Other top officials have left through retirements and resignations, including the Army secretary, Dan Driscoll , who resigned this month after repeated clashes with Hegseth.

When the defence secretary first announced the effort to trim the highest levels of the military ranks, he argued it was intended to remove “redundant force structure to optimise and streamline leadership”. And in a memo released in May 2025, he added that his aim was to free the military from “unnecessary bureaucratic layers”.

At this time last year, Hegseth also declared an end to “woke” culture and announced new directives for troops that included “gender-neutral” or “male-level” standards for physical fitness.

Senator Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, expressed concern over Hegseth’s latest move in a statement. He said eliminating senior leadership positions must be done in consultation with Congress and warned that the planned cuts “should alarm every American”.

“Congress has been clear with the Secretary that he must consult this body and explain his reasoning for senior officer removals and promotion holds. To date, we have not received satisfactory answers,” Reed said.

“Our military is conducting major operations around the world, and the force is already under strain,” he added.

The number of general officer positions is set by law, but positions can be left unfilled if the administration does not submit nominees to Congress.

articles.title: Obama-appointed judge clears way for White employee to challenge Seattle's DEI policies
articles.summary: Joshua Diemert's racial hostile work environment lawsuit against Seattle's DEI programs heads to trial after a unanimous appeals court ruling.
articles.body: A unanimous federal appeals court ruled Monday that a jury should decide whether Seattle's DEI initiatives created a racially hostile work environment for a White employee, while emphasizing that federal anti-discrimination law protects workers regardless of race. The three-judge panel did not rule on whether Seattle's DEI programs violated the Constitution or federal anti-discrimination law. Instead, it found that the allegations were enough to let a jury decide whether the way the city carried out those initiatives created a racially hostile work environment. The ruling leaves the larger constitutional questions about Seattle's race-based programs unanswered. "Workplace training programs designed to address racial barriers are not inherently discriminatory, and nothing in Title VII prohibits employers from either discussing historical and ongoing discrimination against persons of color or seeking to address such discrimination," wrote Judge Mary Murguia, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. "Accordingly, race-conscious training programs may violate Title VII when they create a racially hostile work environment." TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE Joshua Diemert, who worked for Seattle's Human Services Department, alleged that over several years he had been subjected to repeated race-based comments and workplace incidents, including being asked by supervisors what he could contribute "being a straight White male," being told it was "impossible" to discriminate against White people and being encouraged to give up a leadership role so a person of color could be promoted. He also attended DEI trainings where speakers allegedly said "White people are cannibals," that racism is in "White people's DNA" and that "White people are like the devil." Laura D'Agostino, an attorney with Pacific Legal Foundation who argued the case, said the panel ruled only that Diemert lacked standing and did not decide whether Seattle's race-based affinity groups and training programs were constitutional. INDIANA ATTORNEY GENERAL SUES HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS ASSOCIATION OVER RACE-BASED BOARD QUOTA "This decision does not give government employers a green light to classify employees by race. The Ninth Circuit expressly reiterated that government racial classifications are constitutionally suspect and subject to strict scrutiny," D'Agostino said. "It simply concluded that Mr. Diemert had not established the personal injury necessary for the court to reach that constitutional question in his case." D'Agostino said the ruling shows that Title VII does not give protections to racial-equity training when it becomes the source of harassment. "Calling something racial-equity training does not place it outside the protections of federal civil rights law. Employers can address discrimination without creating or tolerating a racially hostile environment for their employees," D'Agostino told Fox News Digital. The court ruled the case wasn't about any one remark or training session. Instead, it concluded a jury should decide whether the alleged comments, DEI trainings and workplace incidents, taken together over several years, created a racially hostile work environment. "The evidence was sufficiently numerous, frequent, and severe that his hostile work environment claims must be decided at trial," D'Agostino said. A spokesperson for the city of Seattle said they are reviewing the decision and discussing potential next steps for the city. WHITE DEVELOPER SUES BALTIMORE MAYOR, CITY COUNCIL CLAIMING HE WAS FIRED BECAUSE OF HIS RACE Ilya Shapiro, of the Manhattan Institute, said the decision leaves constitutional challenges to similar DEI programs on the table despite the standing ruling. "Although the court affirmed the dismissal of Diemert's equal-protection claim, it did so because he didn't present evidence sufficient to show personal injury, not because equal-protection claims aren't viable," Shapiro told Fox News Digital. Shapiro said the "race-conscious" programs are standing on "dubious legal ground." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The decision also reinforced that federal anti-discrimination law applies equally to employees regardless of race. Citing the Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services, the panel noted that Title VII "draws no distinctions between majority-group plaintiffs and minority-group plaintiffs. Eric Wessan, Solicitor General for Iowa, said Monday's ruling is a major wake-up call for DEI classes and trainings across the country, arguing that they breed hostile work environments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think the easiest way to think about it is if the same stuff was happening, but he was another race other than White," Wessan told Fox News Digital. "How obvious would it have been that that was a hostile environment? And I think in this case, the answer is, it would have been pretty obvious." "I'm not surprised that the hostile environment claim can go forward. And that's really important too, because a lot of these DEI policies across the country do create hostile work environments for White employees. And for a long time, there was no pushback against that."

articles.title: Schumer preaches affordability in Dem midterm pitch while sabotaging GOP fixes for soaring costs
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked GOP affordability and permitting reform bills, raising questions about their campaign messaging on cost of living issues.
articles.body: Democrats are pitching themselves as the answer to the economic woes Americans are facing in their pursuit of power in Congress, but they have made a habit of blocking the GOP’s attempts to tackle cost of living issues. Affordability has become the centerpiece of the Democrats' campaign messaging heading into Election Day in November, and they’ve wielded it like a political cudgel that left-wing candidates from Michigan to Texas are using to browbeat Republicans. But in the Senate, it requires cooperation and compromise to tackle those issues, and Republicans say that their colleagues across the aisle have bedeviled that process. They’ll have one last shot Wednesday to address a sliver of the issue with a bill targeting data centers and voters' pocketbooks, but Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus are poised to block it. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY "I think right now, the whole thing is just, you know, play politics with all these issues and get to the election," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital. "I think that, you know, what you're seeing is that this is the party of no, can't take yes for an answer, and is interested in just trying to politicize everything going into the election." When asked if blocking the data center bill, and another that would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, could turn the table on Democrats’ messaging, Thune said, "Well, it makes it pretty hard for Democrats to make that argument." Democrats don’t believe that blocking the bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, would hurt their affordability message, particularly because the legislation lacks teeth — many of the requirements for large-load customers, like data centers, to repay their electricity usage are optional. Schumer trashed the data center bill as being purely politically motivated to bolster a vulnerable candidate staring down a tough race in November against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, even though only three House Democrats voted against it earlier this month. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER "Because we don't vote for frauds," Schumer said when asked why Senate Democrats wouldn't vote for it. "It's voluntary. Not a single company has to comply with it."Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital that if "you guys do your job and explain that the bill does nothing," the political ramifications would be low for Democrats. "It does nothing, and so people know that, but there's more political risk for them than for us," Murphy said. When asked if there was a concern that shutting the bill down could hamper their best weapon on the campaign trail, Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital, "Absolutely not." "The American people can see through just the politics of this. They know that this bill is good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them, because it's not — it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said. REPUBLICANS FEAR THEY ‘HAVEN’T DONE A DAMN THING’ TO LOWER PRICES AHEAD OF MIDTERM RECKONING Not all Democrats want to outright kill the GOP’s latest affordability push, however. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., isn’t totally against allowing the legislation to proceed, but he wants a guarantee from Thune that his bill, the Power for the People Act, would get an amendment vote to add some regulatory heft to the measure. "You want to address the affordability issue, you need to do something real," Van Hollen told Fox News Digital. "As soon as Senator Thune says he'll have a vote on Power for the People Act, then for sure, we should go forward." It’s not the only attempt at grappling with affordability issues that Democrats have sunk, or at least kneecapped, near the finish line before the midterms. Republican leaders wanted to get a deal on permitting reform, which would lower costs on energy projects and reform the regulatory process writ large, on the floor during this final sprint before the election, but Democrats walked away from the deal last week. "I would tell you, all the chemistry, I think, was perfect for getting this deal done," Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who has led the permitting reform push, told Fox News Digital. "And that doesn't happen very often on such a complex issue. So it's very disappointing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The deal is reportedly back on, but won’t be handled until after the election during Congress’ lame duck period, where several agenda items have been punted that may never see the light of day. Still, Republicans will need Democrats to get anything post-election, and the track record of bipartisanship over the near two years that they’ve controlled the chamber has ebbed and flowed. "I mean, we got 53 Republicans, you got to have 60. I’d have busted the filibuster a long time ago, and we would've had a lot more done," Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital. "But we wasted a year and a half of President Trump."

articles.title: Democrats eye Nebraska as an opportunity to take a Senate seat away from Republicans
articles.summary: Democrats hope they might be able to swipe both a Senate and a House seat from Republicans in this solidly red state.
articles.body: OMAHA, Neb. — Marine Corps veteran Gunner Arellano is a Donald Trump man — he voted for the president three times — but, he said, he won’t be casting a ballot for Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., in November. Dan Osborn, an independent who has the backing of the state’s Democratic Party, is “more for the people” than Ricketts, Arellano, a 35-year-old tobacconist, said in an interview at the S.G. Roi cigar shop in downtown Omaha late last month. While Arellano is familiar with Ricketts, a former two-term governor who ranks high on the list of wealthiest senators, he said that the senator isn’t present enough. “All those politicians, they want to come around when it’s election time, right?” he said. “Come down on a Wednesday in the middle of your term, you know.” Arellano said he’ll vote for Osborn, and voters like him are the reason that Democrats in Nebraska and at the national level hope they might be able to swipe a Senate seat in this heavily Republican state. They’re even more optimistic about flipping the state’s Omaha-based 2nd Congressional District, where Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris won in 2024 and Republican Rep. Don Bacon is retiring. In that year, Osborn surprised many political observers by running a competitive campaign against Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., who ended up winning by a little more than 6 percentage points while Trump took the state by 20 points. The latter margin is one reason, along with Ricketts’ record of winning statewide races at the gubernatorial and Senate levels, that Republicans are confident they can keep the seat. Omaha was the last in an eight-stop, five-state tour that NBC News reporters took through battleground congressional districts — and states with competitive Senate races — along Interstate 80 in late August. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take control of the chamber next year, and Nebraska has emerged at the edge of the small list of states that could be in play in November. While there hasn’t been much in the way of independent polling of the state, Republicans are facing into a national wind as Trump’s approval ratings have cratered. Amid the ongoing war with Iran, rising prices for gas and diesel fuel, and Trump tariff policies that have wreaked havoc on rural America, Democrats see a resurgence of a brand of prairie populism that they believe will boost their candidates here in the heartland. That’s why Democrats say they aren’t as worried as they might be about an influx of GOP ad spending on the race, both from Ricketts and outside groups. Since Sept. 1, the Republican side has spent $7 million on the air, with another $8 million booked before Election Day, according to AdImpact data analyzed by NBC News. Osborn and groups backing him have spent $3.5 million and have reserved another $1.5 million. The money differential suggests Republicans are concerned about holding a seat that has been in their hands since 1997 — or at least committed to making sure they don’t take victory for granted. “I think you’re going to see, when Pete starts defining him [Osborn], and some of the outside groups come in to do that, then it’s going to go back to a safe red seat for us,” David McIntosh, president of the Club for Growth, which is backing Ricketts, said in an interview in early September. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party, said in a telephone interview that she believes the money won’t be dispositive because Republicans and Ricketts have worn out their welcome. “Basically, voters are saying, ‘We’re not buying what you’re selling,’” she said. “So it’s not going to matter.” Most Republicans will stick with Ricketts, but some see Osborn as a candidate they will — or could — vote for. “Working man, union guy, seems grounded in the ways of Nebraska, an outsider,” said Chris Holder, 45, of Elkhorn, who works as a business analyst at Union Pacific Railroad. “I haven’t really vetted Osborn a whole bunch, but I am giving him consideration.” It’s an easy sale for Democrats here. Sally Guest, 48, a registered nurse whose husband, Larry, no longer works after an accident, said the two of them, both Democrats, are eager to vote for Osborn. “Pete Ricketts is the millionaire class, and he’s not served Nebraska well,” Sally said. “So I hope we don’t get any more of Pete Ricketts.” The Guests are acutely aware of health insurance costs because of her job and his disability, Sally said. Ricketts voted for Trump-backed legislation that cut back on the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid. The Guests have insurance for him but not for her — she pays for medical care out of pocket — because of the price. “God forbid I have a medical emergency or end up in the emergency room for an accident,” she said. “I’ll have to — I don’t know — I’d be better off dying.” But Todd Going, a business development manager in Omaha, said he plans to vote for Ricketts. A onetime Democrat, the 57-year-old Going said that party’s leftward movement — across the country, not just in Nebraska — makes him wary of voting to give it more power. “There’s been a total flip-flop on what party is representing the working class and the taxpayers,” he said. “And now I see the Democrat Party as totally different than even when I switched. It’s even more so. You see the socialists and the communists thing going on — what’s happening in all these elections all over the country, it’s very concerning to me.” At the House level, all the Republicans who spoke to NBC News said they plan to vote for Brinker Harding, an Omaha city councilman who is trying to re-create the kind of electorate that voted for Bacon three times. National Republicans say it’s a tough race — one of two currently held by Republicans that the Cook Political Report rates as leaning toward Democrats — but they believe Harding is hitting his marks. “Brinker Harding is a business leader and public servant with a record of results in Nebraska who is building a coalition of Republicans, Democrats and independents alike who believe in his vision of common sense over crazy,” Zach Bannon, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said, adding that Harding is “poised to win this November.” His opponent, Democrat Denise Powell, won a crowded primary earlier this year. The Guests said they don’t know much about her, but they will, as Larry put it, “vote blue” in a district that Democrats call the “blue dot” because it sometimes goes for their party in presidential elections while the rest of the state and most neighboring states typically vote Republican red. While Harding is portraying Powell as too extreme for the district, she is tying him as tightly as she can to Trump. So are national Democrats. “Nebraska voters want someone who will go to Congress and fight for them, not another party rubber stamp,” said Madison Andrus, a spokeswoman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, adding that Harding “bends the knee to Donald Trump.”

articles.title: Thune seeks lifeline for 3 embattled Senate GOP incumbents
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is seeking to throw a political lifeline to embattled Republican incumbent Sens. Jon Husted (Ohio), Pete Ricketts (Neb.) and Dan Sullivan (Alaska) by scheduling votes Wednesday on two bills that would address the growth of AI-driven data centers and stock trading by members of Congress. All three GOP senators…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is seeking to throw a political lifeline to embattled Republican incumbent Sens. Jon Husted (Ohio), Pete Ricketts (Neb.) and Dan Sullivan (Alaska) by scheduling votes Wednesday on two bills that would address the growth of AI-driven data centers and stock trading by members of Congress.

All three GOP senators are locked in tough battles, and whether they win or lose in November could determine if Thune remains Senate majority leader in 2027.

Democrats, however, are gearing up to defeat the bills. They argue the reforms are “watered down.”

Sen. Jacky Rosen (Nev.), a centrist Democrat, told The Hill on Tuesday that she’s planning to vote against the data center bill coming to the floor Wednesday, waving it aside as a hastily arranged rescue plan for Husted and other embattled GOP incumbents.

“This bill … has no teeth,” she said. “This is just a pivot.”

She said it “sure seems like” a political bailout for Husted.

“He’s been real friendly to data centers,” she said.

Recent polls show former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) leading Husted by an average of nearly 4 points in the Ohio Senate race.

In Ohio — where 75 percent of voters oppose the construction of data centers in their communities, according to one recent poll — Democratic Senate candidate Brown has tagged Husted as “the face of data centers in Ohio.”

One ad approved by Brown slams Husted for “aggressively recruiting data centers to the state” and “cutting sweetheart tax deals and fast-tracking approvals while ordinary residents watch their electricity bills explode.”

“This is a last-ditch effort for a candidate who is way underwater in his state,” Rosen said, voicing a view shared by other Democratic senators.

Recent polls, meanwhile, show Ricketts in a tight race with Independent candidate Dan Osborn in the Nebraska Senate contest and Sullivan neck and neck with former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) in the Alaska Senate race.

Political prognosticators are increasingly predicting that Democrats could recapture the Senate, even though few handicappers thought that scenario was likely at the start of the election cycle.

Thune has brought two House-passed bills to the floor that will give Husted, Ricketts and Sullivan a chance to argue that they’re responding to voters’ concerns over energy- and water-hungry data centers and lawmakers getting rich on stock trades by voting for legislation to address those issues.

Thune is looking to flip the script in the Ohio, Nebraska and Alaska Senate races, where the GOP incumbents have had to play defense in the face of Democratic attacks.

“It makes it pretty hard for Democrats to make that argument” that Husted is the “face of data centers in Ohio” or that Ricketts and Sullivan are profiting from stock trades if they block the Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act, Thune told reporters.

“These are both broadly bipartisan bills that have passed the House with huge majorities, all of which get at the issues that Democrats seem to find able to use in their campaigns,” he said.

“If you’re really serious about doing something on data centers, then voting for Husted’s bill would be a great solution. And if you’re concerned about members using the knowledge and information they have here in some sort of a financial way, then passing the stock act would be a great way to address it,” he argued.

“Both of those [bills] would literally go to the president’s desk,” he said. “If they get through the Senate, they’re both cleared out of the House. We could send them to the president’s desk.”

The Ratepayer Protection Act, sponsored by Husted, would ask states to consider standards for requiring data centers to pay for the costs of upgrading infrastructure to meet their higher energy consumption needs.

It passed the House overwhelmingly on Sept. 16 by a vote of 417-3, with only three Democrats voting against it.

The other House-passed bill Thune is bringing to the floor is the Stop Insider Trading Act, sponsored by Ricketts.

It would generally prohibit members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from purchasing new stocks and would require public notice before they sell their existing stocks. It includes a provision requiring voters to show photo identification when casting a ballot — a core element of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, one of President Trump’s top priorities — in an effort to address the possibility of voter fraud.

It passed the House in July by a vote of 232-198. Only 13 Democrats voted for the bill.

The Democratic and Independent candidates running against Ricketts and Sullivan have attacked the senators over data centers and the trend of members of Congress getting rich from stock trades.

Osborn, the Independent challenger in Nebraska, has accused Ricketts of profiting from data center construction and criticized him for recruiting — while governor — Facebook to build a data center in Papillion, Neb.

Earlier this month he posted a picture of Ricketts at the groundbreaking for the Facebook data center on social media and commented, “Pete loves data centers,” using the heart emoji for “loves.”

Osborn has also attacked Ricketts for earning an estimated $10 million in the stock market in April 2025, when the market gyrated wildly after Trump announced his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs.

Ricketts touted the upcoming Senate vote on his stock trading bill on social media.

“This week, the Senate is planning to vote on my Stop Insider Trading Act. This bill would ban congressional insider trading. We need to pass this commonsense legislation and restore integrity to Congress,” he posted on Facebook.

Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, has slammed Sullivan for getting “three-times richer” by trading stocks during his Senate career.

She has called for a ban on congressional stock trading.

A new ad from WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with the Senate Democratic leadership, features a narrator who identifies herself as a line cook and bartender criticizing Sullivan for having “nearly quadrupled his net worth” and “cutting healthcare for Alaskans” while in Congress.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is keen to deprive Husted, Ricketts and Sullivan of claiming legislative wins that they could use to shield themselves from attacks on the campaign trail.

“We don’t vote for frauds!” Schumer declared Tuesday, panning the bill that Thune is bringing to the floor that Republicans say would help shield taxpayers from paying higher utilities costs because of data centers.

Schumer slammed the bill as a fake guardrail, even though House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and almost every other House Democrat voted for it earlier this month.

He argued the data center bill “does not require any productions at all” and dismissed it as a “toothless messaging bill.”

The Democratic leader has also pooh-poohed the proposal to limit members of Congress from trading stocks as weak sauce.

“The stock trading bill. They’re doing the same thing on stock trading. All of the sudden the GOP is pretending they care about banning stock trading in Congress,” he said, arguing that last year the House Homeland Security Committee advanced a stronger bipartisan bill.

“Now they watered down the ban and created loophole after loophole in this sham legislation. Let’s be clear, this bill does not ban stock trading. In fact, under this bill, members of Congress could keep stocks they own, sell them and continue trading in privately held companies. What kind of bill is that?” he said.

“The bill doesn’t cover the president,” Schumer noted. “Yet Trump traded more stocks than all of Congress combined.”

Other Democrats indicated that their caucus will vote largely in unison Wednesday to block the bills sponsored by Husted and Ricketts.

“I’m hearing that they’re diluting it,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.). said of the Stop Insider Trading Act. “That’s weak sauce, that’s milquetoast, that’s not what we need to do. We need to stop both sides of the aisle from trading stocks. We need to stop the corruption in Washington.”

“No senator should own individual stocks and this bill I don’t think gets the job done,” he added.

articles.title: GOP breaks with Trump on multiple issues
articles.summary: Republicans in both chambers are increasingly breaking ranks with President Trump across a host of sensitive issues, hoping some separation from the GOP’s unpopular standard bearer will help avert a blue wave in the midterm elections. The divisions are highly unusual for a party that’s walked virtually in lock-step with Trump for more than a…
articles.body:
Republicans in both chambers are increasingly breaking ranks with President Trump across a host of sensitive issues, hoping some separation from the GOP’s unpopular standard bearer will help avert a blue wave in the midterm elections.

The divisions are highly unusual for a party that’s walked virtually in lock-step with Trump for more than a decade. But as the president’s numbers have tanked over the summer and rising costs have squeezed voters of all stripes, more and more Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump’s agenda, if only as a temporary strategy to retain power in the next Congress.

The pushback targets a range of policies, including Trump’s hard line on immigration enforcement; his full-throated embrace of data centers despite the public backlash; his signature tariffs, which have challenged businesses at home and alliances abroad; and his warm reception of Chinese President Xi Jinping during a recent visit to Washington.

But none of those issues seems to resonate quite as much as the cost of gasoline and diesel fuel, which have spiked in response to the global trade disruptions caused by Trump’s decision to launch a war with Iran earlier in the year. Even the top GOP leaders on Capitol Hill have been forced to acknowledge that Trump’s agenda, which was once their winning ticket, has become a liability heading into November.

“What’s happening in Iran [has] sort of trumped everything else that’s going on,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told Fox News on Monday.

Weeks ahead of the midterms, gas prices are hovering just below $4.50 per gallon, diesel sits near $6.50 and Republicans are feeling the heat from angry voters at home. The trend is even affecting traditional GOP strongholds, including the deepest red parts of the Midwest, where farmers are being crushed by a combination of high fuel costs, high fertilizer costs and trade policies that have curtailed U.S. exports on certain crops.

The Iran war has been a major factor in driving these high prices, both physically impeding the transport and processing of oil and other goods and generating anxiety among commodities traders.

As the election gets closer and prices grow higher, even top Republicans are calling for the war to come to a close.

“It’s been a priority and an objective of every administration, for 50 years nearly, to ensure that Iran didn’t have a nuclear capability. Now that’s done. Operation Epic Fury was an epic success. … The world is safer because of it,” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said in an interview with a local TV station last week.

“But now we’ve got to bring that to a resolution,” Johnson said.

“I think that’s been a bit of a disappointment to the American people, that we aren’t at the end, especially when they see gas prices going up,” said Senate Republican Policy Chair Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.) this week.

The problem is especially acute for Republicans in tough races, who have supported the Iran conflict for much of the year but are now changing their tune in the last legs of the campaign.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is running for a Senate seat, wrote last week on X. She’s calling for an “immediate end” to the conflict.

However, the White House itself is standing behind the war, with Trump describing it as a small price to pay for preventing a nuclear Iran.

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done. Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more,” Trump said at a recent rally in North Carolina.

Fuel prices and Iran are not the only topics seeing daylight between Trump and Republicans heading into November.

The president recently welcomed Xi to Washington with a red-carpet greeting and a lavish state dinner, even as China has supplied Iran with military support against U.S. forces. Those dynamics have sparked criticism from some Republicans in the Capitol, who wanted to see Trump confront the Chinese president more forcefully.

“Is it appropriate that you welcome him? Yeah,” said Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska). “But it’s equally appropriate that you ask him really tough questions.”

Public anger over data centers is also fueling the internal divisions. The centers are wildly unpopular among voters in both parties, leading a number of Republicans to call for new limits on their construction. But Trump has hammered those critics, warning that any restrictions would only cripple the United States in the global race AI dominance.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump posted last month on Truth Social, which he owns.

Immigration is emerging as yet another fault line within the GOP. Trump’s aggressive deportation policies have been cheered by his base, but they’ve also alienated many Hispanic voters who have shifted their support back to Democrats. To counter that shift, some vulnerable Republicans are now attacking Trump on the issue, saying he went “too far.”

“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) said in an explosive campaign ad directed straight at Trump.

Trump, who had endorsed Salazar, responded by reposting messages calling for her defeat.

Republican strategist Doug Heye told The Hill that Trump is a “hindrance” to Republicans because “his poll numbers are dragging Republicans down up and down the ballot” and “taking Republicans off message on the issues of affordability by creating a daily outrage du jour.”

He said that disagreeing with Trump could be part of Republicans’ election strategy and that “they need to be talking about the issues that voters are talking about.”

Meanwhile, there also appears to be division within the GOP about how to handle the diesel situation in particular.

Rural-area Republicans are increasingly calling for a ban on diesel exports to mitigate the impacts of the situation on the nation’s farmers.

“While our farmers are filling tanks at record prices and families are being impacted by affordability every day, we are still shipping diesel overseas,” Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) said Monday in a statement. “That is backwards.”

However, recent economic analyses have found that while banning diesel exports could temporarily bring down the price of that fuel in the U.S., it could ultimately raise gas prices since the two are often produced together and refineries would have less incentive to run with limited shipping options for their diesel.

The White House has offered mixed messages on the issue, with Trump initially backing a diesel export ban but Energy Secretary Chris Wright indicating that the administration will not support one.

“We’re trying to avoid a blunt hammer of a government policy, understanding the complexity of refining,” Wright told The Wall Street Journal .
