articles.title: Pritzker’s weight loss prompts discussion on changing attitudes over presidential appearance
articles.summary: JB Pritzker is looking different these days. Illinois’s Democratic governor, who is considering a 2028 run for president, admitted as much when he acknowledged he lost 80 pounds after using a GLP-1 in the last two years to help treat his diabetes. Pritzker’s weight loss journey has been so apparent in recent months that the governor felt the…
articles.body:
JB Pritzker is looking different these days.

Illinois’s Democratic governor, who is considering a 2028 run for president, admitted as much when he acknowledged he lost 80 pounds after using a GLP-1 in the last two years to help treat his diabetes.

Pritzker’s weight loss journey has been so apparent in recent months that the governor felt the need to address it in a personal essay and in a couple of interviews. In those sit-downs, he explained that it was health concerns — not his political pursuits — that prompted the effort.

But among political observers, the change renewed a discussion on how presidential candidates present themselves to voters, particularly in an era when authenticity — or at least the appearance of it — matters more than ever.

Politicians are shooting their own videos and swapping television studios for less formal podcasts. They’re wearing less makeup, dressing in casual clothes or sporting hair pulled back in a ponytail — all as part of an effort to appear less packaged.

For presidential candidates, the way they present themselves can convey something beyond aesthetics and vanity. Voters can make judgments about a candidate’s health and vitality, particularly after a political cycle when age and mental acuity became such a big part of the narrative around former President Biden.

“What people look like does matter to voters,” said Democratic strategist Jamal Simmons, even as he noted that “in the modern era, our old ways of thinking about it may be wrong.”

“People are looking for candidates that don’t fit the traditional mold,” he said. “That may also be true physically.”

Still, Simmons added, “being healthy, having stamina and an ability to work nonstop at a frantic pace is required regardless of the aesthetics. Candidates have to be healthy enough to work at a pace that is unreal to most people.”

In an interview with “CBS Mornings” last week, Pritzker acknowledged the chatter that his weight loss is directly tied to preparing for a presidential run. But he said his reasoning was personal.

“I’ve been driven my whole life to lose weight,” Pritzker said. “The fact that I am now able to do it because this GLP-1 became available is truly like, I mean, it’s something that has meant a lot to me.”

Other high-profile candidates — including Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D), who ran as the vice presidential nominee in the 2024 presidential election — have slimmed down in recent months, Axios noted in late 2025. And former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who is known for his youthful appearance, has sported a beard, something he attributes to being out of public office.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), another 2028 contender, has long been known for his looks and polished appearance, something his allies say is a net positive.

“Appearance does matter when people are voting for president of the most powerful nation on earth,” said Garry South, who served as an adviser to Newsom in his first gubernatorial campaign. He added that “aesthetics do play a role, rightly or wrongly, in politics.”

Appearance is something voters have mentioned in focus groups, said South, a Democrat who argued that Trump is the first “obese” commander in chief since former Presidents William Howard Taft and Grover Cleveland.

“In both cases that was more than 100 years ago [and] we haven’t had a bald president since [former President] Eisenhower at the dawn of the TV age,” he added.

At the same time, some Democrats argue that Newsom’s well-coiffed image could be a caricature used against him. One strategist pointed to the Harper’s Bazaar photo shoot he did with then-wife Kimberly Guilfoyle in 2004, where the couple sprawled on a rug, with a headline that blared “The New Kennedys.”

“It’s definitely in the top five things that will be thrown against him,” one strategist said. “You can definitely see, ‘Out of touch, pretty boy who poses for weird photo shoots and dines at French Laundry’ as part of that oppo book.”

Trump has frequently targeted Pritzker on his weight, at one point last year calling him a “big, fat slob.”

But unlike many of his presidential predecessors, Trump has never embraced regular workouts and has been known to eat fast food. Former President Clinton jogged regularly and even had a treadmill in his room when he traveled. Former President George W. Bush was an avid runner, and former President Obama hit the gym each morning.

Laurie Essig, the chair of gender, sexuality and feminist studies at Middlebury College, said appearance does matter and those impressions date back to the late 19th century, particularly with men and their bodies.

“I think it does. I think Donald Trump is the exception to that rule,” Essig said. “What we want is someone who works hard and has an investment in bodily discipline.

“We associate fat with moral failing,” she continued, while throwing cold water on those opinions. “These cultural biases are deep and longstanding,”

Pritzker himself said he has his own views on the matter, and said he doesn’t agree that a candidate’s appearance alone should matter.

“I think it’s more like the content of your character matters more, and I’ve always believed that,” he said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times. “And that’s why I haven’t listened to people who say nasty things about me being overweight.”

articles.title: Schmitt faces fallout after debunked Jack Smith narrative
articles.summary: Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) is facing accusations he tried to launch a conspiracy tying former special counsel Jack Smith to others who prosecuted President Trump — a line of questioning that unwound when the senator apparently confused two basketball teams. Schmitt seemed poised for a gotcha moment with Smith when he asked him if he…
articles.body:
Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) is facing accusations he tried to launch a conspiracy tying former special counsel Jack Smith to others who prosecuted President Trump — a line of questioning that unwound when the senator apparently confused two basketball teams.

Schmitt seemed poised for a gotcha moment with Smith when he asked him if he ever attended a February 2024 NBA game in Atlanta where the Hawks played the Golden State Warriors.

Schmitt gave a sly smile when Smith first denied attending the game and later implied he was catching the prosecutor by surprise.

“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff. So I’ll give you a second to process it, so you don’t, you know, perjure yourself,” Schmitt said.

His staff displayed a poster of texts of Smith’s staff discussing seat numbers, and Schmitt said “for context” the date of the game was just after Fulton County, Ga., District Attorney Fani Willis (D) acknowledged a romance with a staffer — drama that rocked the case into Trump’s election interference in Georgia.

But the demeanors of the two men changed over the course of the exchange, with Smith becoming increasingly confused and Schmitt’s staff swiftly removing a poster featuring the text exchange the senator implied proved the prosecutor’s travels.

MS NOW zoomed in on Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.), seated next to Schmitt, with a stunned look on her face as Smith recalled he had attended a game in Maryland where the Iowa Hawkeyes were playing.

It soon became clear that Schmitt and his staff had confused Smith’s attendance at an Iowa Hawkeyes basketball game for an Atlanta Hawks game.

Democrats have accused Schmitt of fomenting a conspiracy theory. Schmitt, despite the apparent mistake and flawed premise as well as the public criticism, has since promoted the inquiry on conservative media.

“Somebody didn’t do their homework,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) told The Hill.

“I’m a trial lawyer by profession. You get it right, or don’t do it.”

The episode was arguably terrible timing for Schmitt professionally, coming just hours after Axios reported the Missouri Republican could be a possible contender to be a running mate to Vice President Vance should he run for president in 2028.

Schmitt ended his line of questioning by calling Smith “a dirtbag.”

“You may think you’re a hero in this story, but let me tell you something. You’re the villain,” he told the prosecutor.

Smith acknowledged attending a Hawkeyes women’s basketball game that featured the star player Caitlin Clark, saying he went when the Iowa team traveled to Maryland. Footage of the game where he was spotted in the crowd has since circulated on social media.

“If this is the correct basketball game, I recall going to a University of Maryland basketball game where Caitlin Clark was playing right around that time. … You could check if that was the exact date it was Maryland playing Iowa, I think February of 2024,” Smith said.

Democrats see something more insidious behind the mix-up.

“We were witness to a narrative, a false narrative of accusing you of being at a game that you were nowhere near, and I suppose that was supposed to be in furtherance of some sort of conspiracy or something,” Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) said during the hearing.

“I really don’t know, but you would hope that members of this committee would not make those kinds of accusations — and then to call you names on top of that.”

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) said the information Schmitt had was “just wrong” and that he’s glad Smith was able to “set the record straight.”

“To show a witness a document and then not let them see it is a terrible practice, but then also not to know the facts is a bigger problem,” Schiff said.

“It looked like he had text messages suggesting that Jack Smith was at some sporting event he wasn’t at, and he hoped to catch Jack Smith in some false statement,” Schiff added. “It turns out the only thing false was the presentation.”

Schmitt’s team did not respond to a request for comment, including questions about what he was attempting to allege.

Even besides not being in Atlanta, Smith said he never met Willis or her associate Nathan Wade during his time as special counsel. The timing of the game would also have little nexus with news breaking of their affair.

“I presented him with text messages about him wanting to meet with people that could have obviously been related to the prosecution that was coordinated with his office in Atlanta,” Schmitt said.

The idea made Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) chuckle.

“Going to a basketball game? That’s a sketchy activity for a prosecutor,” he joked. “Nefarious things are going on.”

“The mysteries of that line of questioning will remain obscure and may be known only to the questioner. I couldn’t figure it out — put it that way,” Welch said.

In the conservative podcast world, however, Schmitt has championed the interaction, while other since-deleted posts from conservative media initially celebrated an exchange apparently flagged for them in advance.

Schmitt discussed the exchange during an appearance on “The Charlie Kirk Show,” which included a recap based almost entirely on snippets of the senator speaking and did not show Smith denying his attendance at the Atlanta game. Schmitt briefly mentions Smith “claimed” he was at another game but stressed the Hawks game was the only professional match happening in Atlanta.

Conservative influencer Benny Johnson posted — then deleted — a post saying Schmitt “just CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself” and said the senator “pulled out the receipts.”

Screenshots are circulating indicating Fox News host Sean Hannity also deleted a social post saying Schmitt “puts Smith on the spot” during the hearing.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) said Schmitt’s questioning was part of a broader “ham-handed” effort to misrepresent Smith’s investigation.

“The general objective of the majority in today’s hearing seemed to be to smear Jack Smith and to misrepresent his investigation, his priorities, his values, from the first questioning to the last,” he said.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) accused the committee’s Republicans of “gaslighting” the public.

“This committee’s Republicans are more concerned with Trump than the truth, more concerned with Trump’s crimes than the Constitution. And I’m watching today people say, ‘Oh, this is an unprecedented investigation. This man did unprecedented things.’ Heck yeah he did unprecedented things, because when has the United States of America seen people storm the Capitol and try to stop the peaceful transfer of power,” he said during the hearing.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) tangled the most with Schmitt over his dialogue, pushing him to once again display the poster showing the texts so that Smith would have a chance to respond.

Schmitt fumed at Klobuchar for igniting an “open session” about his questions and accused her of “trying to rehabilitate the witness.”

She later fact-checked the sports schedule.

“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. The Iowa Hawkeyes played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93 to 85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored 30 points, so it must have been a pretty good game. The game was, in fact, in Maryland,” she said.

“For a U.S. senator to have false information and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology.”

articles.title: US faces another major Middle East troop withdrawal, but threat remains
articles.summary: About 2,500 U.S. troops had remained in Iraq as part of Operation Inherent Resolve, but Baghdad's effort to disarm Iran-backed militias remains unfinished.
articles.body: The U.S. military is scheduled to end its mission in Iraq on Wednesday, bringing to a close a military operation that has lasted more than two decades — despite an ongoing war in Iran sparked earlier this year. The Iraq mission began with the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein and later evolved into a campaign to help Iraqi forces defeat the Islamic State group after the terrorist organization's rapid rise across Iraq and Syria. In recent years, however, the remaining U.S. military presence has increasingly served as both a counterweight to Iran's influence and a frequent target of Iran-backed militias. The Iraq agreement was reached before the U.S. and Iran entered direct conflict earlier this year and under a different administration and military leadership — leaving the final phase of the withdrawal to unfold in a dramatically different security environment than the one envisioned when the timeline was negotiated. TRUMP REVEALS WHEN US MILITARY WILL LEAVE IRAQ AFTER 23-YEAR MISSION The deadline stems from an agreement reached by Washington and Baghdad in 2024 under President Joe Biden to wind down the U.S.-led coalition's military mission after Iraqi officials concluded their security forces were increasingly capable of handling the fight against ISIS. It follows the U.S. military's 2021 departure from Afghanistan, also under the Biden administration, which ended another two-decade American war and left no U.S. troops in the country. The withdrawal, however, was chaotic, widely viewed as "botched" and resulted in the deaths of 13 U.S. service members and dozens of civilians. HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY The Pentagon declined to confirm to Fox News Digital whether the timeline remains on track or provide details about any continuing U.S. military involvement in Iraq after Wednesday. The Iraqi Embassy did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment. The danger to U.S. forces persisted through the final months of the mission. Army Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, was killed at Erbil Air Base in July during the controlled detonation of a downed Iranian attack drone. About 2,500 U.S. troops had remained in Iraq as part of Operation Inherent Resolve, the U.S.-led coalition established in 2014 after ISIS seized large swaths of Iraq and Syria. American forces had previously withdrawn from Iraq in 2011 before returning three years later to help Iraqi and partner forces combat the terrorist group. That threat has since diminished significantly. The Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessed this summer that ISIS in Iraq "almost certainly remains severely degraded," focused largely on its own survival and unable to capitalize on instability from the war with Iran, according to the latest Lead Inspector General report on Operation Inherent Resolve. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper told lawmakers in May that ISIS attacks in Iraq and Syria had fallen 70% since 2023 and were at their lowest level since 2013. The U.S. mission had already shifted accordingly. Rather than routinely fighting alongside Iraqi forces, American troops increasingly trained, advised and provided intelligence to local forces expected to carry out counterterrorism operations with limited or no direct U.S. involvement. The Pentagon also began moving the infrastructure for that fight out of Iraq. Operation Inherent Resolve shifted its headquarters to Amman, Jordan, this year, allowing U.S. personnel and assets to redeploy while Iraqi forces assumed greater responsibility for counterterrorism operations. But the declining ISIS threat has coincided with a different challenge for Baghdad: powerful Iran-backed armed groups that have resisted efforts to surrender their weapons. US-BACKED EFFORT TO DISARM IRAQ’S IRAN-LINKED MILITIAS HITS SETBACK, EXPERTS SAY The Iraqi government had initially sought to bring armed groups operating outside state control to heel by the same Sept. 30 deadline. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi argued that the departure of U.S. forces would eliminate a key justification for the militias to remain armed. Several powerful Iran-backed groups, however, have resisted calls to disarm. Two prominent factions initially agreed to surrender their weapons by the deadline, while other armed groups refused, according to a U.S. government report released this summer. Baghdad has since pushed back its timeline. Zaidi said last week that the government now aims to complete the process by June 30, 2027, beginning with a 90-day period in which armed groups would halt attacks in exchange for assurances that U.S. forces would not target them. The groups would then gradually surrender their weapons or be brought under state control. The holdouts remain heavily armed. U.S. military officials said the groups retain rockets, missiles, drones and, in some cases, air defense systems capable of threatening American personnel and facilities across the region. The DIA reported that Iran-aligned militias launched hundreds of attacks on U.S. forces and diplomatic facilities in Iraq after the war with Iran began. articles.title: Liberal stronghold set to adopt eye-popping minimum wage amid business exodus
articles.summary: Seattle's minimum wage is set to hit $22.14 in 2027 as 450 restaurants closed in early 2025, and job postings dropped 35% since February 2020.
articles.body: Seattle is slated to increase its minimum wage to $22.14 an hour in 2027 as the broader metro area contends with a sharp drop in job openings and Seattle businesses face mounting cost pressures. Beginning in 2025, all Seattle employers, including small businesses, were required to pay the same minimum wage, which is adjusted annually for inflation. Several Seattle restaurant owners who have since closed their businesses have cited rising labor costs among the financial pressures that contributed to their decisions. During the first half of 2025, shortly after the wage hikes went into effect for all businesses, 450 Seattle restaurants — about 16% of the city’s total — closed. Restaurant and retail transactions fell by as much as 7% over the prior year in some business and shopping districts around Amazon and Microsoft campuses, according to Square data cited by The Wall Street Journal. SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS If no other jurisdictions increase their minimum wages to match or surpass Seattle, the Emerald City will have the highest minimum wage in the country next year. An individual working full-time on minimum wage in the city will make just over $46,000 annually. "If the servers are making $20 an hour, then I gotta pay the cooks $35," one Seattle restaurant owner said of the wage increases to Eater in 2024. LA HOTEL LEADERS WARN MAYOR BASS' $30 WAGE MANDATE IS KILLING BUSINESS AHEAD OF WORLD CUP, OLYMPICS "Operators are making less money than ever and are charging more than ever," Anthony Anton, CEO of the Washington Hospitality Association, said last year, according to The Center Square. A peer-reviewed study published by researchers at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, found that the mere announcement of Seattle’s minimum wage increase decreased the formation of new businesses in city limits while actually increasing the founding of new businesses in adjacent suburbs with lower wage floors. Proponents of Seattle's minimum wage increase, however, argue that the city's high cost of living necessitates higher pay for those on the lower end of the economic spectrum to avoid more people falling into poverty. They also claim that higher pay can help businesses with staff retention. DOWNTOWN SEATTLE LOST 30,000 JOBS, BILLIONS IN OFFICE VALUE SINCE 2020 PAYROLL TAX: NEW REPORT FINDS Seattle's degrading business environment predates the widespread implementation of its inflation-indexed minimum wage laws. From the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 to 2023, about 500 local businesses closed, according to the Downtown Seattle Association. A year later, the association counted 543 vacant storefronts in the city. During this period, many business owners cited property crime as well as local economic factors as the reasoning behind their exits. Declining business formation comes at an inopportune time for Seattle residents as job postings in the city’s metropolitan area fell by 35% between February 2020 and October 2025, a decline second only to San Francisco, according to an Axios analysis. Local business owners have reported that individuals with master's degrees, and those with experience at prestigious companies such as Microsoft, are applying to work as baristas. Seattle’s once-booming tech-driven economy is now showing clear signs of strain, from weaker hiring to elevated downtown office vacancies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As of the fourth quarter of 2025, 35.6% of Seattle’s downtown office space was vacant, up from 32.3% the year before, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. Some iconic Seattle businesses, Starbucks, for example, have shifted operations away from the city.

articles.title: Brookings confirms what basic economics predicted about Biden’s open border
articles.summary: The Biden administration ran an unhedged book for four years. The results were higher rents, suppressed wages at the low end of the distribution, school systems absorbing students they hadn’t budgeted for, emergency rooms eating uncompensated care.
articles.body:
The Brookings Institution released a study last week confirming something that anyone with a semester of economics could have told you four years ago: When a government floods a housing-constrained country with millions of additional people in a short period, rents go up.

Congratulations to the researchers for formalizing what every landlord and renter in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Chicago had figured out by 2022.

The paper , titled “How Did the Post-Pandemic Migration Surge Affect Labor and Housing Markets?” examined major U.S. metropolitan areas from 2021 through 2024. The authors estimate the country absorbed roughly 6.5 million people above pre-pandemic migration trends during that period. Their conclusions: metropolitan rents rose an estimated 1.4 percent to 1.6 percent, and average hourly wages across the entire workforce may have dropped by up to 1.5 percent, as large numbers of new arrivals entered the lower end of the wage distribution. Native-born workers fared somewhat better. Their wages actually rose on net by 0.9 percent, and metropolitan GDP climbed by 1.5 percent.

In short, rents went up, average wages went down and GDP gains were concentrated among those already here. Better than nothing, I suppose.

I have spent 30 years in institutional finance, working alongside some of the most sophisticated investors in the world. Risk management isn’t complicated: You price the position before you open it, not after you have closed it at a loss.

The Biden administration ran an unhedged book for four years. The results were higher rents, suppressed wages at the low end of the distribution, school systems absorbing students they hadn’t budgeted for, emergency rooms eating uncompensated care.

The exposures were obvious going in, but the administration refused to mark them. Now Brookings has done it for them. But the economics are the polite part of this story.

While American renters were paying more for apartments they could barely afford, Mexican cartels were having a record run. Congressional materials attributed to Homeland Security Investigations put cartel-linked human smuggling revenues at roughly $13 billion in 2021 alone. Applied across the full four Biden years, that suggests something in the neighborhood of $50 billion, though no official audited total exists and the true figure remains elusive.

What is certain is the business model: control the territory, charge fees of $8,000 to $20,000 per crossing depending on the route, and exploit anyone who can’t pay.

DEA’s 2025 Project Portero specifically targets the cartel gatekeepers who controlled those corridors. As Associated Press reporting from 2024 documented, migrants had become “the most lucrative commodity” for criminal groups competing for control of migration and drug-smuggling routes in southern Mexico. That tells you everything you need to know about what four years of open borders actually financed.

And there was plenty to study. In fiscal year 2024, the Justice Department filed 146 federal trafficking cases against 223 suspected traffickers , including 136 principally associated with sex-trafficking. Those are just the prosecuted cases, a fraction of the underlying activity.

Homeland Security reported more than 2,700 alleged Tren de Aragua arrests in its 2025 enforcement figures. The same criminal networks that charged migrants for border access moved fentanyl through the same corridors, generating a separate catastrophe that did not require a Brookings study to document.

Then there are the children. The House Oversight Committee reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra’s department lost track of hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied migrant children, who were placed with questionable sponsors during the Biden years. Children entered federal government custody and then disappeared from federal government awareness. The agency tasked with their welfare treated them as a logistics problem that it couldn’t be bothered to solve.

Nobody wanted to touch the public health angle to this, either. During the same years Americans were required to show vaccine credentials to enter a restaurant or return from international travel, millions of unvetted and likely unvaccinated people crossed the southern border with no health screening at all. COVID spread, as did other diseases, and those eager to blame Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy cannot explain the timing behind recent outbreaks. A more detailed study is needed of the effect of millions of unvetted individuals, most likely unvaccinated, rapidly pouring over the border.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommend post-arrival evaluations covering communicable disease screening, immunization assessment, and connection to primary care. But that implementation would have required personnel, planning, and a basic admission that there was a problem — none of which the Biden administration was willing to provide.

The Brookings authors note, correctly, that the numbers on paper aren’t all bad. Native employment held steady throughout the border crisis. GDP grew and native wages rose modestly on aggregate.

But those figures comfort nobody in Houston neighborhoods where rents climbed year-over-year, or in school districts absorbing hundreds or thousands of new students they weren’t staffed up to teach.

Aggregate data always flatters policy, but the specific households, communities and children bear the actual costs.

Here is what none of these studies will tell you: We didn’t need new laws. Congress wrote the relevant immigration statutes decades ago. We needed a president willing to enforce them and a leadership team committed to treating cartel smuggling networks as the organized criminal enterprises they actually are, not as a political inconvenience to minimize until after the next election.

Credible border enforcement, timely legal processing, and aggressive prosecution of criminal networks profiting from both the drugs and the people are not cruel policies. They are what a functioning government owes its constituents.

The solutions were never secret. The political will was just missing.

In January 2025, we got a president who refused to accept that framing. Upon his taking office, illegal border crossings nearly stopped overnight . The economics were never complicated. Neither was the solution.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management. He writes about issues in finance, constitutional law, national security, human nature, and public policy.

articles.title: Vance cozies up to MAHA movement

At the end of a fireside chat on…
articles.body:
For the second year running, Vice President Vance headlined the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement’s annual summit in Washington, D.C.

At the end of a fireside chat on Tuesday, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked Vance why Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio gets all the “good memes.”

“We get tremendous support for the MAHA agenda from the White House, but from nowhere as much as the vice president’s office, and I want to thank you for that, for your commitment to our country and to our children,” Kennedy said to applause.

The exchange was a not-so-veiled allusion to the jockeying for the 2028 presidential race playing out between President Trump ’s top aides, even as neither Vance or Rubio have made their White House aspirations officials.

And it highlights the key role that Kennedy’s MAHA movement will play in efforts to consolidate the coalition that helped Trump win in 2024.

During their conversation, Vance referenced his decision to take up a “carnivore” diet recommended by Kennedy that consists of meat and fermented foods such as sauerkraut while avoiding alcohol and many sugary foods. He’s one of several members of the administration who adopted the diet.

“I called Bobby and… [say], ‘Hey man, I’m thinking of giving up sugar for Lent. What are the health benefits of giving up sugar?’ And he’s like ‘No, no, no. Have I got the thing for you,’” Vance said. “And that was Fat Tuesday, and thanks to Bobby Kennedy, Fat Wednesday never came.”

The MAHA movement only embraced Trump after Kennedy dropped his Democratic presidential run against Joe Biden , launched an independent campaign then eventually dropped that and became a key GOP surrogate.

Trump ultimately credited the MAHA movement with giving a boost to his own MAGA movement and helping him win the election, rewarding Kennedy with the HHS post despite his outspoken history of vaccine skepticism.

Kennedy has pressed ahead with some priorities, such as rolling back vaccine recommendations for children.

But the alliance has been rocky at times, particularly after the Trump administration moved to expand production of a dangerous pesticide.

MAHA advocates have warned the GOP could lose its strength within the movement unless it shores up support for its voters, and there’s some signs that Democrats are looking to seize on the tensions.

Democrats who are also critical of the chemical industry have leaned into what they view as a possible alliance with MAHA. Earlier this year, they jumped at the opportunity to grill Kennedy during congressional hearings following the president’s executive order prioritizing the domestic production of glyphosate, a key ingredient in the controversial herbicide Roundup.

On Tuesday, Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed launched a new health platform called “Building a Healthier America Policy Agenda,” which seeks accountability for polluters and backs legislation allowing people to sue pesticide manufacturers over harms caused by their products, CBS News reported .

More than one third of the American public identifies as MAHA supporters, and roughly two thirds of them lean Republican, according to polling from the spring . But some Democrats think it’s not a foregone conclusion that MAHA backers will vote GOP.

“I think we have an opportunity to remind folks that we’ve always been the people who want people to be healthier, rather than the folks who capitulate to the food, ag and pharmaceutical corporations that are too often on the wrong side of things,” El-Sayed told CBS.

Vance and Kennedy played up areas in which the administration can be aligned with MAHA, such as with the use of AI to push back on advice given by medical experts, and the fight against fraud within health and social support system — another Vance priority.

Back at the White House, Rubio joined other Trump officials in rolling out America.gov.

Just last month, Rubio was asked about his own eating habits on Katie Miller ’s podcast. He admitted to straying from Kennedy’s carnivore and ferments diet.

“The Pop-Tart is one of the great American innovations in history,” Rubio said.

“I’m not gonna travel the world with a cooler full of sauerkraut,” he added.

The Supreme Court declined to stop the execution of a Tennessee woman who is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection this morning at 10 a.m. Christa Pike is set to be the first woman executed by the state of Tennessee in 200 years.

The Senate is scheduled to vote today on two key bills addressing the growth of AI-driven data centers and stock trading by members of Congress, both of which Democrats are planning to defeat as they see them as “watered-down” reforms. The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports on how the votes could serve as a lifeline for three embattled Senate Republican incumbents.

The Treasury Department will automatically enroll millions of children in the administration’s Trump Accounts under new rules, eliminating the need for parents to sign up for the program. About 7 million have been registered so far, and more than 60 million accounts will be created for other children under 18.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walks along the Colonnade before President Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping at the White House, Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press)

HEGSETH’S OVERHAUL : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to announce a 20 percent cut to positions at the Pentagon for admirals and generals in his latest push to overhaul the Department of Defense (DOD), two Pentagon officials confirmed to The Hill’s Filip Timotija .

The cuts will affect senior leadership positions across the Army, Navy and Air Force, Timotija reported.

Hegseth will discuss the workforce reductions, along with his other priorities in the coming months, during his State of the Force address today at the Marine Corps base in Quantico, Va., where he will speak before junior officers and enlisted leaders.

In another move to shake up the status quo at DOD, Hegseth yesterday directed departments to halt appointments of civilian staff to tenured positions at U.S. military service academies (MSAs) and develop hiring plans that prioritize “institutional flexibility and faculty contribution to the warfighting mission.”

In a one-page memo titled “Refocusing the Military Service Academies on Warfighter Education,” Hegseth said the institutions’ chief purpose is to prepare young officers to eventually lead the U.S. military, and he said granting tenure undermines that goal.

“To ensure our educational institutions remain firmly focused on this warfighting mission, we must address the structural mechanisms that have allowed civilian academic norms to dilute our focus on lethality,” Hegseth wrote in the memo.

Granting tenure to civilian faculty, he added, “contributes to curriculum that drifts from the mission of educating our warfighters to the research priorities of the tenured academics.”

It was not immediately clear what would happen to faculty currently tenured.

Hegseth said last year his goal was to replace “woke” civilian professors with military personnel.

IN THE HOTSEAT : Former special counsel Jack Smith parried questions and insults from GOP lawmakers as he testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday about his decisionmaking overseeing investigations into the president.

Smith strongly defended his work in the cases investigating Trump’s retention of classified and sensitive documents at Mar-a-Lago and his conduct related to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, saying they were a result of the president’s own actions.

But the panel’s Republicans tore into Smith, accusing him of pursuing partisan prosecutions against Trump.

“You will go down as a total dirtbag,” said Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.).

One of the most contentious issues was Smith’s obtaining of the call logs of a dozen Republican senators as part of his Jan. 6 investigation. Tuesday was the first time that they had a chance to challenge him directly on the subpoenas.

Smith defended the subpoenas as necessary to map out communication, while Republicans accused him of violating their privacy and the Speech and Debate Clause of the Constitution, which protects lawmakers from legal scrutiny for official legislative acts.

The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports on the takeaways from the testy hearing. Read more here .

‘ MORALLY BINDING’: Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) announced that key artificial intelligence industry leaders signed on to a pledge to build “robust” internal controls a nd layers of auditing in an effort to appease the public’s concerns about AI development.

The agreement lays out a series of voluntary commitments for AI developers, according to Johnson, but Trump described “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence Joint Commitment on Frontier SI Responsibilities,” as “morally binding” and “almost like a constitution.”

“There’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect,” Trump said in a rare White House North Lawn appearance, joined by tech executives including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , OpenAI president Greg Brockman , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , Google CEO Sundar Pichai , Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk .

Zuckerberg described the commitments as “good steps forward” and “a start” for the industry, saying, “The basic idea is that we want to give the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works in the way that we intend.”

While the agreement marks a point of collaboration between Trump and several AI leaders, as The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro and Julia Shapero report for Insider, Huang is one of the few standing behind the president’s full-steam-ahead approach to AI.

Earlier in the day, Trump launched a website, America.gov, that uses AI to help Americans navigate federal government websites and find information and services they need.

GO AHEAD, FOR NOW : The Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can resume its policy of deporting migrants to countries that they have no ties to for the time being as the court considers the policy’s legality.

The emergency ruling Tuesday lifts the restrictions imposed by a district court judge, who found the individuals affected don’t have a sufficient opportunity to raise claims that they would face torture if deported to a third country. The high court announced it would hear arguments in the case in December before issuing a final decision.

The court’s three liberal justices said they would’ve kept the limits in place while they consider the case. None of the justices explained their reasoning.

Third-country removals have been a key part of Trump’s strict crackdown on illegal immigration. His administration has signed many agreements with countries around the world to accept deportees, many of them in Africa.

HEALTHCARE SPENDING CLIFF: Billions of dollars appropriated for health programs are at risk of expiring today — the final day of the fiscal year — because the Trump administration has refused to spend the funds.

The administration’s refusal to use the money presents a major test for Congress, The Hill’s Nathaniel Weixel reports. Democrats and even some Republican lawmakers say refusing to spend the appropriated funds is illegal.

Weixel takes a look at some of the funding at risk of expiring if the country reaches the end of the fiscal year without a resolution.

Congressional leaders have been warning for more than a month that the Trump administration is sitting on more than $1 billion for global health initiatives.

Congress appropriated $9.4 billion for global health programs for the fiscal year that ends today. The Trump administration has spent all but the $1.3 billion intended to go toward protecting maternal and child health, and countering infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis.

Of the $101 million appropriated for the Teen Pregnancy Prevention (TPP) program, the Department of Health and Human Services has only spent roughly $500,000. The program funds organizations that educate young people about how to make healthy choices to reduce risky sexual behavior and prevent sexually transmitted infections and unintended teen pregnancy.

TPP has long been targeted by conservatives, and the administration has said it wanted to reshape TPP to embrace an abstinence-only curriculum. Trump’s 2027 budget request calls for cutting the program, but the 2026 budget preserved the program and its funding.

NOO CANADA : The president’s ban on $1 billion of Canadian goods went into effect Tuesday, the latest escalation in the trade war with the U.S. and its northern neighbor.

The restrictions apply to Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages. Trump signed executive orders to implement the bans earlier this month, the same day that retaliatory Canadian tariffs on $27.6 billion of American goods took effect.

Trump cited Canadian “discrimination” against U.S. dairy, motor vehicles and alcohol as his rationale for the bans.

The U.S. and Canada have been locked in an increasingly tense trade war for weeks, kicked off by Trump’s move to implement 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s government vowed to match those tariffs “dollar for dollar.”

Trump and Carney have traded barbs amid the conflict, with the president calling Canada “one of the worst countries in the entire world” in comments to reporters Monday.

Carney has responded to the tensions by increasing his country’s ties to Europe, even expressing some openness to the idea of becoming the European Union’s first associate member. He told the European Parliament earlier this month that his country and Europe are “stronger together.”

Trump’s tariffs will be under the spotlight today in the U.S. Court of International Trade as the judges consider whether the president has the authority to levy them under the Trade Act of 1974.

articles.title: Schmitt on mix-up at Jack Smith hearing: ‘My job is to ask questions’
articles.summary: Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) on Tuesday reflected on his mix-up during former special counsel Jack Smith’s hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, saying his job “is to ask questions.” Schmitt asked Smith if he attended a February 2024 NBC game in Atlanta between the Hawks and the Golden State Warriors. articles.body:
Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) on Tuesday reflected on his mix-up during former special counsel Jack Smith’s hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, saying his job “is to ask questions.”

Schmitt asked Smith if he attended a February 2024 NBC game in Atlanta between the Hawks and the Golden State Warriors. It quickly became clear that there was confusion about the game, after he appeared to mistake the Iowa Hawkeyes for the Hawks.

“We had information, of course, about him being at a basketball game,” the Missouri Republican told Nexstar affiliate KTVI St. Louis later Tuesday. “The only NBA game going on that night was in Atlanta on Feb. 2 of 2024. His team had talked about that. He answered the question.”

“My job is to ask the questions, and his job is to answer the questions,” he added.

Schmitt accused Smith of previously lying to lawmakers but acknowledged that the former federal prosecutor’s reply about which game he attended “is what it is.”

“But I guess the one thing that Jack Smith and I can maybe agree on is that we’re a fan of college sports and college basketball,” the senator said with a smile.

He also claimed that Smith went to Atlanta to meet with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (D), who investigated President Trump’s alleged attempt to subvert former President Biden’s 2020 election win in Georgia. Willis indicted Trump and 18 others with racketeering charges in 2023. The case was later dropped .

Schmitt seemed puzzled during the hearing when Smith said he did not recall going to Atlanta during that time period and that he did not meet Willis. The exchange continued as the senator’s staffers showed a poster board with texts sent between Smith and Willis, which they swiftly took down.

The incident led to more confusion not just from Smith but from other lawmakers present, including Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.). The former special counsel recalled attending an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland to watch Caitlin Clark play.

Schmitt’s questioning ended with the lawmaker calling Smith a “villain” and “dirtbag.”

He answered TMZ’s questions about the mix-up after following the hearing, giving similar responses to what he told KTVI St. Louis, before being asked how the “mistake” happened.

“It’s not a mistake,” the senator replied. “I asked him if he was in Atlanta. The only NBA game going on –– actually, the only NCAA men’s game or NBC game with a 7:30 tip-off was in Atlanta, so I asked him if he was in Atlanta that night.”

TMZ pressed him further, referring to photos and video of Smith watching the Hawkeyes.

“For that night? Great,” the Republican replied. “Well, then he was at the Hawkeyes game. I just asked him if he was in Atlanta.”

Klobuchar slammed Schmitt for the flub and said Smith was owed an apology.

“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith,” the Minnesota Democrat said. “The Iowa Hawkeyes played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93-85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over 30 points, so it must have been a pretty good game.”

articles.title: America’s balance between national security and press freedom depends on trust
articles.summary: People are drawing a line between restrictions tied to a concrete danger and those that look politically motivated.
articles.body:
When President Trump recently sought to ban three news outlets from the White House , he mentioned national security concerns as one explanation for why he felt the move was warranted.

National security is one area where Americans are willing to compromise on press freedom. But they do not always take such claims at face value.

Overall, Americans unquestionably value press freedom. But for most people, that comes with certain limits they think journalists should abide by — particularly around national security.

For instance, most Americans say news organizations should not publish classified details about military operations during an active conflict. And a majority say the U.S. government should be able to require a news organization to take down a story if it poses a national security risk.

These findings come from our new survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative on views of press freedom. Although this study was conducted before Trump’s recent actions — which have been temporarily blocked by a federal judge — it speaks to a longstanding point of friction: Where should Americans draw the line between press freedom and national security?

It may seem natural, even unsurprising, that people don’t want to risk the lives of U.S. troops or civilians. At the same time, our findings sit in tension with a core First Amendment principle: that the government shouldn’t have the power to censor speech and the press.

Americans certainly are not voicing a blanket rejection of press freedom in general. A large majority say that freedom of the press is extremely or very important to the well-being of society. And just 10 percent say the government should have the power to get a news story removed because it’s critical of the government.

People are drawing a line between restrictions tied to a concrete danger and those that look politically motivated. Focus group participants who were a part of this study saw this nuance.

“I mean, a lot of these things could put people’s lives in danger,” said one right-leaning man in his 30s. “Military, CIA, anyone undercover, any military. We don’t know whose lives could be at danger for this. I think there’s a reason why it’s classified. It shouldn’t be distributed.”

A right-leaning woman in her 40s offered another perspective: “I would agree that if it was truly something that would put our country or anybody in danger, that would be totally wrong for them to publish that. However, can we trust completely that it does have to do with national security concerns? Or is this person a whistleblower, and it’s something we really should know, but they’re putting it under the blanket of ‘this is a security concern?’”

Pentagon restrictions on press access had been getting attention around when the focus groups were conducted in late May and early June. While the government also mentioned national security concerns in that case, a left-leaning man in his 50s expressed skepticism.

“Who’s the source that’s telling me that it’s an emergency?” he said. “They’re citing national security concerns. How many emergencies have we had since our current president took office? Something like 27 emergencies? Like, everything’s an emergency? To me, it’s just another opportunity to clamp down on the press.”

In many ways, these views — and feelings toward the actors involved — are seen through a partisan lens.

Republicans are considerably more likely than Democrats to say the government should be able to nix a news story to protect national security (72 percent versus 50 percent). And 60 percent of Republicans say it is never acceptable to publish classified details about military operations during an active conflict, compared with 35 percent of Democrats. These figures include independents who lean toward each party.

Democrats have become far more concerned about potential restrictions on press freedom since Trump returned to office, and 72 percent say the press has become less free during Trump’s second term. In this context, they are not as comfortable letting the government make judgments about what news should be suppressed.

Republicans largely don’t seem to want this power in the hands of journalists: Their trust in news organizations has declined substantially over the past decade , and 74 percent describe most journalists as “biased.”

The military, meanwhile, benefits from a bipartisan reservoir of trust that few other American institutions enjoy. In an October 2025 Pew Research Center survey , 75 percent of U.S. adults said they have confidence in the military to act in the public’s best interest — a far higher share than say the same about journalists (47 percent) and elected officials (27 percent). That baseline trust may make Americans more willing to defer to the government’s judgment when national security is invoked, even if they’re otherwise wary of giving officials broad power over the press.

Americans aren’t simply picking a side in an abstract freedom-versus-safety debate, and most aren’t reflexively pro- or anti-censorship. They are reasoning through it, case by case.

This reasoning depends in part on trust: trust that the person invoking national security is doing so in good faith, and that the journalists reporting on these issues are doing so responsibly. Americans don’t extend both kinds of trust equally.

Many Americans of both parties are comfortable prioritizing national security over press freedom in principle. What’s clear is that it’s not as simple in practice.

Katerina Eva Matsa is the director of news and information research at Pew Research Center , where Michael Lipka is an associate director of research .

articles.title: What to watch in Supreme Court’s new term

articles.body:
Watch The Gavel Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 3 p.m. EDT as Zach and Sophie unpack the upcoming Supreme Court term. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions. Tune in!

The Supreme Court’s term begins Monday, and it’s set to be another big one.

President Trump’s agenda. Guns. Climate. Religious rights. LGBTQ protections.

And, of course, curveballs to come out of the impending midterm elections.

There’s a lot to unpack. Here are five key questions we’re watching as we get into the term:

This past term, Trump’s record at the Supreme Court was mixed.

He picked up some key wins on the emergency docket, particularly in the final weeks: The justices allowed White House ballroom construction to continue and a key immigration database to be overhauled before the midterms.

But it was far from a clean sweep, and on the merits docket, Trump lost many of the cases he cared about most.

The justices found his birthright citizenship restrictions unconstitutional. They ruled his “Liberation Day” tariffs illegal. They said he didn’t give Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook enough due process before sacking her.

As he’s failed to convince the courts on those agenda items, Trump has more regularly won when he’s advanced the long-sought goals of the mainstream conservative legal movement. Just look at how Trump eviscerated for-cause firing protections at independent agencies, a cause conservative groups had pushed for years. The president merely teed up the Supreme Court to take the swing.

Heading into the new term, the justices on Tuesday announced they’re already adding a big Trump policy to their docket.

In December, they’ll take the bench to consider whether the president’s third-country deportation policy is legal.

More could be added in the coming weeks.

The administration has appealed cases concerning its mandatory detention of certain immigrants, suspended University of California research funding, the Department of Government Efficiency, Trump’s Day 1 asylum ban, the Pentagon’s transgender troops ban, the executive’s authority to appoint acting U.S. attorneys and more.

Is this a blockbuster moment for the energy industry?

Ask any court watcher what the most anticipated and possibly consequential case of the upcoming term is, and they’ll likely point to the one being heard first: Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County.

ExxonMobil and Suncor are hoping to block a lawsuit brought against them by the local government in Boulder, Colo., by arguing that federal law, such as the Clean Air Act, preempts state-level claims that aim to hold energy companies liable for the effects of climate change.

The city and county sued the two companies in April 2018, seeking billions of dollars in damages over allegations that they misled the public and sold fossil fuels at levels that they knew would contribute to greenhouse gas emissions.

The outcome would likely impact dozens of other similar pending or future lawsuits nationwide. A broad ruling in favor of the energy giants could nullify those, while a decision for Boulder could open the courthouse doors to more challenges.

And the ripple effects may not stop there.

Legal analysts say the ruling could reshape corporate liability across a range of industries, creating a litmus test for state-level authority on issues beyond climate change.

Take artificial intelligence, for example. Companies could use a decision siding with Suncor and ExxonMobil to argue that state and local regulations should be invalidated because only the federal government can put guardrails on the technology.

When the justices sit for their first oral argument, it’ll be less than a month before the midterm election. And they’ll have already weighed in on some critical issues.

So far this summer, the Supreme Court has blocked Missouri Republicans from holding the election under a more favorable set of congressional lines and struck down the Trump administration’s proposed restrictions on mail-in voting.

The justices have allowed the use of a revamped immigration database to check individuals on state voter rolls. They’ve also lifted a ruling that prevented party committees from accessing cheaper advertising rates in the lead-up to November.

There’s at least one more on the emergency docket yet to be decided: Whether Delaware can require political organizations, such as Americans for Prosperity, to publicly disclose their donors.

Other election-related disputes are already in the pipeline, with justices agreeing to review a lower court ruling that blocked key parts of an Arizona law requiring documentary proof-of-citizenship to register to vote.

The case, Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, is scheduled for oral argument in December.

Whether other questions arise that warrant the court’s intervention remains to be seen, though experts note that emergency applications are a fixture of every major election cycle.

How momentous of a term will it be for the Second Amendment?

The Second Amendment is front and center as the justices hear arguments in December on whether states can ban AR-15s and other guns they deem “assault weapons.”

It’s the latest test of the conservative majority’s expanded Second Amendment test that requires gun control measures to be consistent with the nation’s historical tradition.

The high court has since taken up cases clarifying who may carry guns (see here and here ) and where they may carry them (see here ).

This term, they’ll delve into what guns are protected.

Roughly a dozen states’ assault weapons bans hang in the balance.

This week, the justices are mulling the Trump administration’s request to take up whether the government can ban felons from possessing a gun.

It would mark a blockbuster case — it’s one of the most prosecuted federal crimes in the country.

It would also put the Trump administration at odds with some gun rights advocates, as the administration is defending the statute as constitutional.

So far, the Supreme Court has declined to get involved. It’s had plenty of opportunities but has often punted, sending cases back for another look in light of recent opinions.

Gun rights groups are bringing plenty of new cases to the justices, too. Challenges to Minnesota’s gun licensing regime, Maryland’s gun restrictions and New York’s stun gun ban all are inching closer.

Is more still coming on the religion docket?

A major religious dispute is already on the docket. Many court watchers think another one is incoming.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has asked the justices to review a Texas law that mandates the display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.

The ACLU says the law “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”

The justices won’t decide whether to hear the case until later this fall, but when we ask attorneys what cases they think the court will be taking up, this one is a frequent response.

As we wait, the justices have already agreed to hear a dispute that could lead them to shake up another major religious precedent.

The court will decide whether Colorado can require Catholic preschools to admit LGBTQ families to receive state universal preschool funding.

Colorado doesn’t have a great track record. The court in recent years ruled against its “conversion therapy” ban and sided with a web designer and cake baker who separately challenged a state anti-discrimination law.

Some of those cases centered on free speech. Now, the fight has turned back to religion.

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Strike three: The Supreme Court has rejected the use of a House map that would have given Missouri Republicans a pickup opportunity in the midterms for the third time. The state must use the 6-2 map design in November, the justices said.

Another blow for prediction markets: Kalshi has taken another hit after the 6 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that states can regulate prediction markets like gambling platforms. It is the second appellate-level loss for Kalshi in the last month.

Iowa pollster ruling appealed: Trump is appealing a federal judge’s dismissal of his lawsuit against an Iowa pollster and the Des Moines Register over a poll published days before the 2024 election that showed former Vice President Kamala Harris with a 3-point lead in the presidential race.

New York climate law struck down, again: A second federal judge has struck down New York’s “Climate Superfund” law, which sought to hold fossil fuel companies financially liable for contributing to climate change.

Judge rejects federal counterterrorism grant conditions: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cannot force states to change their election administration practices by threatening to withhold federal counterterrorism funding, a federal judge in D.C. has ruled.

Former special counsel Jack Smith testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday for over four hours as Republican lawmakers continue to probe his investigations of Trump in the Mar-a-Lago documents and Jan. 6 cases.

Judge Leslie Southwick , a George W. Bush appointee, is stepping back from the 5 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals after nearly two decades on the bench. Read more from Bloomberg Law .

A federal bribery case involving D.C. Council member Trayon White has ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked. The Ward 8 councilman was spotted tuning into a council breakfast meeting from federal court last week.

2 conservatives to watch in SCOTUS climate arguments

In conversations discussing the upcoming Supreme Court term, court watchers keep telling us the same thing: Watch two conservative justices as the court kicks off its term on Monday with major arguments implicating the energy industry.

Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil will argue that federal law preempts a wave of state-court suits alleging they contributed to climate change and must pay billions. Colorado’s top court allowed a suit filed by Boulder to proceed; the justices are reviewing whether that was in error.

But potentially unfortunate for the companies, they’ll be facing Justice Clarence Thomas and Justice Neil Gorsuch.

Yes, they are members of the conservative majority and have ruled against left-leaning climate interests in other cases. But the two haven’t been friendly faces for those trying to argue implied federal preemption, like the companies will.

In 2019 , the two agreed that the federal Atomic Energy Act didn’t preempt a Virginia uranium mining ban.

“Invoking some brooding federal interest or appealing to a judicial policy preference should never be enough to win preemption of a state law,” Gorsuch cautioned at the time.

The next year , the duo called on the court to abandon some of its preemption jurisprudence. Thomas has long described some of the court’s past decisions invalidating state laws as “judicial guesswork.”

“The founding generation treated conflicts between federal and state laws as implied repeals… Then, as now, courts disfavored repeals by implication,” Thomas wrote.

Their votes are becoming even more important now that Justice Samuel Alito , another member of the conservative majority, recused from the case on Monday.

A justice typically recuses at the onset of a case, but Alito had participated in the vote to take it up. His new announcement came suddenly and without explanation, though it did happen to land the same day as the justices met behind closed doors for their first scheduled meeting of the new term.

Alito has long held financial interests in the oil and gas sector, but he doesn’t own stocks directly in Suncor Energy or ExxonMobil. The court did not return The Gavel’s request for comment seeking clarity.

His exit came much to the delight of left-leaning groups that have long pushed the conservative justice to step aside from hot-button energy cases.

“Even without Alito’s involvement in this case, the culture of loyalty to corporate powers is ever-present in the Roberts Court,” Court Accountability CEO Alex Aronson said in a statement.

“This loyalty leaves us with polluted water, toxic air, and communities that face the constant threat of natural disasters,” Aronson continued. “Corporations have invested in a favorable outcome in Suncor, and the Roberts Court will make sure to give them their money’s worth.”

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases we are keeping a close eye on…

The Supreme Court’s new term is nearly here. The justices met Monday and voted on new cases to take up. That initial meeting was a big one. The justices confronted roughly 900 petitions to accept cases that piled up over the summer. Court watchers nickname it the “long conference.” We’ve gone through the petition list. Here at The Gavel, we’re previewing cases that could pique the justices’ interest along with other interesting ones. In our third and final week of previews, we’ll focus on business-related cases.

Some cases the Supreme Court heard previously are back for another round:

Corporate Transparency Act: Business interests want the Supreme Court to declare that the Corporate Transparency Act — which requires some businesses to report their ownership to the government — exceeds Congress’ power to regulate interstate commerce and violates the Fourth Amendment’s protections against warrantless searches. The court previously intervened on its emergency docket to reinstate the law. The cases are National Small Business Association v. Bessent and Texas Top Cop Shop, Inc. v. Blanche.

Mortgage escrow interest: In 2024, the justices said an appeals court too easily struck down New York’s mandate that lenders pay interest on mortgage-escrow funds. The appeals court has again found the mandate is preempted by federal law, so the case is back. It’s called Cantero v. Bank of America, N.A. Two other appeals courts have come out the other way, and those cases have reached the justices as well: Citizens Bank, N.A. v. Conti and Flagstar Bank, N.A. v. Kivett .

Commerce Clause: The Supreme Court heard this case in 2023 . Now, it’s back, but with a different legal issue. Norfolk Southern wants the justices to rule that it can’t be hauled into Pennsylvania’s courts solely because it registered to do business there. It says Pennsylvania’s rules unconstitutionally burden other states’ commerce . The case is Norfolk Southern Railway Company v. Mallory .

Several others deal with judges certifying that a lawsuit can proceed as a class-action:

Zillow stock: Real estate marketplace Zillow appeals a ruling that certified a class over allegations the company made misrepresentations about its “iBuying” business, keeping its stock price artificially inflated and later causing it to drop. The case raises thorny questions about the proper legal standards in such disputes. The case is Zillow Group, Inc., v. Jaeger.

Unclaimed Sunoco interest: Sunoco was ordered to pay $100 million for failing to pay oil well interest owners, but a lot of the class were unidentifiable owners. So, those proceeds went to unclaimed property funds. Sunoco says the courts shouldn’t have certified the class. The case is Sunoco, Inc. v. Cline .

United vaccine policy: United Airlines wants to reverse the class certification in a Title VII employment-discrimination lawsuit over its COVID-19 vaccine policy. Federal rules require class-action lawsuits to present a “common question” that applies to class members. United says that isn’t met here. The case is United Airlines v. Kincannon .

TV retransmission fees: Nexstar Media Group, which owns The Hill, seeks to dismiss DirecTV’s suit concerning TV retransmission fees. DirecTV alleges price fixing, but Nexstar says the company shouldn’t have legal standing because it didn’t actually purchase the allegedly price-fixed programming. The case is Nexstar Media Group Inc. v. DirecTV LLC .

Superfund: Canadian mining company Teck Metals wants to end a lawsuit filed by a Native American tribe under the nation’s Superfund law concerning alleged contamination to the Upper Columbia River. The tribe seeks to recover money for the cultural loss it experienced from the incident, a claim the company says shouldn’t be permitted. The case is Teck Metals v. Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservatio n.

Antitrust: Pharma giants AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi want to throw out a revived suit over their efforts to restrict 340B drug-discount practices. It raises questions over an Supreme Court antitrust precedent dating back to 1977. The case is AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Mosaic Health Inc. The justices are also mulling another petition, United Biologics LLC v. Amerigroup Tennessee Inc., which raises questions about the same precedent.

Madoff foreign investors: The fallout of Bernie Madoff’s fraud isn’t done yet. Liquidators seeking to recover funds for investors in foreign funds that lost billions in Madoff’s Ponzi scheme want to reverse a decision involving their claims and bankruptcy law. The case is Fairfield Sentry Ltd. v Citibank NA London .

Bankruptcy & arbitration: Two people who had an account with Marcus by Goldman Sachs claim the bank violated the automatic pause on pending litigation that commenced when it filed for bankruptcy protection. They want damages, but Goldman claims it has an agreement requiring the dispute be arbitrated. The lower courts refused to honor it, and the bank appealed. The case is Goldman Sachs Bank v. Brown .

The U.S. Court of International Trade will hear arguments over whether Trump’s latest round of sweeping tariffs is lawful.

A federal judge in Texas will hold a hearing to decide whether Wilber Rafael Garces Perez , a Venezuelan migrant shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin earlier this month, should be deported.

A federal judge in Seattle will hold a hearing in a lawsuit filed by Roger Rogoff challenging Trump’s decision to abruptly fire him as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington.

A federal judge in Fresno, Calif., will hear arguments as the Trump administration seeks to dismiss a lawsuit brought by a nonbinary Yosemite National Park ranger who was fired after unfurling a transgender pride flag on the El Capitan summit on their day off.

Former Rep. David Rivera (R-Fla.) will be sentenced in Miami after being convicted in May of secretly lobbying on behalf of the Venezuelan government

The Supreme Court will open its new term with oral arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a blockbuster climate case , and Johnson v. United States Congress, a veteran benefits dispute .

Cole Thomas Allen , the man charged with attempting to assassinate Trump at the White House Correspondents Association dinner this spring, will appear in a federal courtroom in D.C. for a status conference.

The Supreme Court will hold oral arguments in Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee, a case implicating retirement plan lawsuits .

The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals will hold oral arguments in a lawsuit filed by the National Association of the Deaf and two of its members over the White House’s decision to stop providing sign language interpreters at press briefings and public events.

A federal judge in Maryland will hold a hearing to resolve all remaining issues in the case of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national and Maryland resident who has been fighting his unlawful deportation.
